title: Dumb and Dumber
logline: Two idiots drive cross-country to return a briefcase. Broad physical and stupidity comedy.
overview: Lloyd and Harry are two men whose stupidity is really indescribable. When Mary, a beautiful woman, loses an important suitcase with money before she leaves for Aspen, the two friends (who have found the suitcase) decide to return it to her. After some "adventures" they finally get to Aspen where, using the lost money they live it up and fight for Mary's heart.
tagline: For Harry and Lloyd, every day is a no-brainer.

jokes.text: That's a lovely accent you have. New Jersey? Austria.
jokes.setup: Lloyd compliments the man's accent and confidently guesses 'New Jersey'
jokes.punchline: The man corrects him — it's Austrian. Lloyd's guess was maximally wrong in a funny direction.
jokes.explanation: Economical and well-structured misdirection. Lloyd's clueless confidence in guessing 'New Jersey' for a thick Austrian accent is a perfect character beat — it establishes his oblivious stupidity immediately. The two-line exchange does a lot of work efficiently.

jokes.text: Austria! Ha ha! Well, then... (puts on Australian accent) G'day, mate. Let's put another shrimp on the barbie.
jokes.setup: Lloyd is corrected that the accent is Austrian, not New Jersey
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to doing a bad Australian accent, confusing Austria with Australia — a classic idiot mistake delivered with full confidence
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully tight escalation on joke 1. The Austria/Australia confusion is a classic dumb-person error, but it's executed with perfect character logic: Lloyd isn't embarrassed by the correction, he just recalibrates wrongly and barrels forward. 'Let's put another shrimp on the barbie' is iconic. The Austrian man's flat 'Let's not' is the perfect straight-man button.

jokes.text: Let's not.
jokes.setup: Lloyd does an Australian accent and says 'Let's put another shrimp on the barbie'
jokes.punchline: The Austrian man responds with two dry words: 'Let's not.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words that do enormous comedic work as a straight-man button to Lloyd's absurdity. The flatness of the refusal is funnier than any elaborate rebuke would be.

jokes.text: Harry feeding gourmet dogs with French service ('Bon appetit, Stella. Oui oui') while driving the Mutt Cutts van, treating show dogs like VIP clients
jokes.setup: Harry is a limo driver — except for dogs, in a van shaped like a giant dog
jokes.punchline: He runs the dog-feeding service with the full ceremony of a fine dining experience: French phrases, individual names, dramatic presentation of hot dogs
jokes.explanation: The gap between Harry's sincere professionalism and the absurdity of the situation (gourmet dog feeding in a van shaped like a dog) is a great slow-burn character joke. The French affectations are a nice touch of unearned pretension.

jokes.text: Suck me sideways.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just experienced a near-collision or traffic incident (tires screech, Whew)
jokes.punchline: His reaction to the incident is the bizarre, nonsensical exclamation 'Suck me sideways'
jokes.explanation: A perfectly absurd piece of Lloyd-flavored vernacular. It's funny because it's so specific and strange — not a recognizable expression, just pure Lloyd. High quotability for how weird it is.

jokes.text: Lloyd's fumbling, stuttering reaction upon seeing Mary for the first time — 'Uh-uh-uh... uh... uh-uh-uh...'
jokes.setup: Mary Swanson appears; Lloyd is supposed to be a professional limo driver
jokes.punchline: He completely loses all function — verbal and presumably physical — reduced to incoherent stammering in front of a pretty woman
jokes.explanation: A reliable physical comedy beat that works because Jim Carrey's physical commitment elevates standard 'man sees pretty woman' comedy. The character integration is good — this is precisely how Lloyd Christmas would react. Not original but executed well.

jokes.text: Why are you going to the airport? Flying somewhere? How'd you guess? I saw your luggage. Then when I noticed the airline ticket, I put two and two together.
jokes.setup: Mary is at an airport with luggage and a ticket; Lloyd asks her why she's going there
jokes.punchline: He explains his reasoning as if it took real detective work — 'I saw your luggage. Then when I noticed the airline ticket, I put two and two together' — treating the blindingly obvious as a brilliant deduction
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. The structure is perfect: asking a pointlessly obvious question, then narrating the 'detective process' behind his conclusion as if it took effort. 'I put two and two together' as the button is excellent — it's a phrase that implies complexity but was applied to the most self-evident situation imaginable. Great character integration: this is precisely Lloyd's brand of confident obliviousness.

jokes.text: So where're you headed? Aspen. Mmm... California. Beautiful.
jokes.setup: Lloyd asks where Mary is headed; she says 'Aspen'
jokes.punchline: Lloyd responds 'California. Beautiful.' — either mishearing her or not knowing where Aspen is, and approving of his own wrong answer with admiration
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. Lloyd gets the destination wrong (Aspen is in Colorado, not California), then congratulates himself on knowing it. The 'Beautiful' as a satisfied sign-off on his own error is a great character detail. Very economical — four words carry the full joke.

jokes.text: Name's Christmas, Lloyd Christmas.
jokes.setup: Lloyd introduces himself to Mary
jokes.punchline: He delivers the introduction in a James Bond 'Bond, James Bond' cadence, completely unironically, with the name 'Lloyd Christmas' — which deflates the suave delivery instantly
jokes.explanation: The Bond parody works because Lloyd is completely oblivious to the gap between his self-image and reality. 'Lloyd Christmas' is an inherently funny name for someone trying to be suave.

jokes.text: This isn't my real job, you know. No? Nope, my friend Harry and I are saving up our money to open our own pet store. I got worms. I beg your pardon? That's what we're going to call it... I Got Worms.
jokes.setup: Lloyd mentions their future pet store; then says 'I got worms' as an apparent non sequitur that sounds like a confession of a personal ailment
jokes.punchline: The store will be called 'I Got Worms' — it specializes in worm farms
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent joke. The misdirection is perfectly engineered: 'I got worms' dropped mid-conversation reads completely as a gross overshare (a medical admission), Mary's 'I beg your pardon?' captures the audience's reaction, and then the reveal that it's a business name is both logical within the film's world and absurd. The added layer that this is their DREAM — a worm farm store — adds to the comedy. This is a cut above standard misdirection; the structure is tight and the reveal is satisfying.

jokes.text: Statistically, they say you're more likely to get killed on the way to the airport, you know, like in a head-on crash or flying off a cliff or getting trapped under a gas truck... That's the worst. I have this cousin... well, I had this cousin.
jokes.setup: Mary is nervous about her flight; Lloyd tries to reassure her with statistics
jokes.punchline: He lists increasingly horrifying ways to die en route to the airport, then accidentally reveals his cousin died in one of these ways — 'I had this cousin'
jokes.explanation: A great escalating dark comedy moment. Lloyd is trying to comfort Mary while actively terrifying her — the cluelessness is perfect character integration. The 'I had this cousin' correction is a lovely dark button. The escalating list of deaths ('head-on crash... flying off a cliff... trapped under a gas truck') keeps building the discomfort.

jokes.text: Oh. Yeah. Good thinking. Can't be too careful. A lot of bad drivers out there. (tires screeching)
jokes.setup: Mary asks Lloyd to watch the road because he's been talking instead of driving
jokes.punchline: Lloyd agrees with her, then lectures about 'bad drivers' while apparently immediately nearly crashing again (tires screech)
jokes.explanation: The hypocrisy payoff is immediate and well-timed. Lloyd agreeing that bad drivers are dangerous while BEING one, capped by the screech of tires, is a tight ironic callback with good character integration.

jokes.text: Okay, gang, you know the rules... no humping, no pushing, no sniffing heinies.
jokes.setup: Harry arrives at the dog show, speaking to the show dogs in the van
jokes.punchline: He delivers pre-show rules to the dogs as if they're athletes in a locker room, with the rules being specifically dog behaviors stated with the gravity of serious instructions
jokes.explanation: A compact, quotable character joke. The specificity of 'no sniffing heinies' alongside 'no humping' and 'no pushing' (a relatively normal instruction between the other two) gives it a nice rhythm. Harry's sincerity makes it work.

jokes.text: Don't worry about a thing, Mrs. Neugy-burger. Neugeboren! Neug-neug-neug... Boren! Boren.
jokes.setup: An angry dog show client confronts Harry about the late dogs
jokes.punchline: Harry mispronounces her name badly, gets corrected, tries again, fails to even get through it, and then finally echoes just the second syllable after she breaks it down for him
jokes.explanation: Classic dumb-character name-mispronunciation comedy. The escalation of failure — 'Neugy-burger' then breaking down at 'Neug-neug-neug' — is a solid comedic structure. The repeated correction by Mrs. Neugeboren, increasingly exasperated, is good straight-man work.

jokes.text: These pooches aren't going to need any primping. You know why? I'll tell you why. Because I bathed them and I clipped them myself. And I stand by my performance.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Neugeboren complains she won't have time to primp the dogs because Harry arrived late
jokes.punchline: Harry boasts that the dogs don't need primping because he personally groomed them — with the implication (confirmed by the whimpering dogs and the follow-up) that he did a terrible job
jokes.explanation: 'I stand by my performance' is a great turn of phrase for someone who's done a visibly terrible job — it's the confidence of someone with no self-awareness. Character integration is strong; Harry's earnest pride in his amateur grooming is very him.

jokes.text: You know, on second thought, you might just want to run a comb through 'em.
jokes.setup: Harry just confidently declared the dogs don't need any primping because he groomed them himself; whimpering dogs are presumably revealed
jokes.punchline: After apparently seeing the dogs himself (or the client's reaction), he immediately backtracks with the understatement of the century
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed understatement that immediately deflates Harry's previous bravado. The pivot from 'I stand by my performance' to 'you might just want to run a comb through 'em' is a great comedic about-face. Economy is excellent — the joke is fully delivered in one mild sentence that implies catastrophic grooming results.

jokes.text: Oh no, Mary. I couldn't possibly accept that, not after all we've been through.
jokes.setup: Mary offers Lloyd a tip; they have known each other for one limo ride
jokes.punchline: Lloyd refuses the tip as if they have a deep, meaningful romantic history — 'not after all we've been through' — when they've just met
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-structured character joke. Lloyd's delusion about the significance of their brief relationship is perfectly captured in that one phrase. 'All we've been through' applied to a single limo ride is a great gap between Lloyd's inner life and reality.

jokes.text: Hey. How about a hug? [airport PA continues] Oh. I hate goodbyes.
jokes.setup: Mary thanks Lloyd and is about to leave; Lloyd pushes for more emotional farewell
jokes.punchline: He asks for a hug at the airport curb, drawing out a goodbye with someone who clearly just wants to leave, and sighs 'I hate goodbyes' as if this is a profound mutual loss
jokes.explanation: A reliable cringe beat. Lloyd's emotional investment in a one-sided connection is very much his character. 'I hate goodbyes' lands well as a sincere delivery of an absurd emotional claim.

jokes.text: (voice wavering) Be strong.
jokes.setup: Mary has gone into the airport; Lloyd watches her leave with enormous emotional investment
jokes.punchline: He talks himself through the grief of her departure with 'Be strong' in a cracking, failing voice — the pep talk is completely undermined by its own delivery
jokes.explanation: Two words carrying a lot of comedic weight. 'Be strong' spoken in a voice already breaking is a perfect self-contradicting moment. It's a Carrey vehicle but the writing sets it up beautifully.

jokes.text: # Goodbye, my lo... # ugh!
jokes.setup: Lloyd, in a heightened emotional state about Mary leaving, begins singing a romantic farewell song at the airport
jokes.punchline: He's immediately hit by something (presumably a door or a bag) mid-song — an abrupt physical interruption of his dramatic farewell moment
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of romantic singing cut off by slapstick injury is a classic but well-executed gag. The setup builds Lloyd's emotional investment only to deflate it with brutal physical comedy. The timing implied by the transcript is good.

jokes.text: Move it or lose it, sister!
jokes.setup: Lloyd is rushing through the crowded airport trying to catch Mary
jokes.punchline: He shouts 'Move it or lose it, sister!' at someone in his way — a surprisingly assertive and rude demand from a character who was just weeping at the departure
jokes.explanation: A quick energy shift that works because of the contrast with Lloyd's weeping state moments before. Not particularly clever writing but the character moment and line delivery would land.

jokes.text: Eenie... meenie... minie... mo! [runs the wrong way, presumably] Hold that plane! Sir, you can't go in there! It's okay! I'm a limo driver!
jokes.setup: Lloyd arrives at a fork in the airport and needs to decide which gate to go to
jokes.punchline: He uses 'eenie meenie minie mo' to make the critical decision, then when blocked by security uses his limo driver status as if it's official credentials
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. 'It's okay! I'm a limo driver!' as a credential to bypass airport security is a perfect encapsulation of Lloyd's character — his total failure to understand the world combined with absolute confidence. The eenie-meenie decision-making for a critical choice is also great character logic. This is highly quotable and very rewatchable. Scores 8+ because it's exceptional character integration with a great quotable line.

jokes.text: Eenie... meenie... minie... mo! [Lloyd chooses which gate to run through by playing eenie meenie minie mo]
jokes.setup: Lloyd is at a split in airport gates trying to figure out which way Mary went
jokes.punchline: He resolves the navigation problem with a children's counting game — no logic applied whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Perfect expression of Lloyd's decision-making process under pressure. The pacing — stretched out for maximum absurdity — works well. Character integration is high: the eenie-meenie approach is exactly what Lloyd would do.

jokes.text: Hi, Lloyd. Hi, Harry. How was your day? Not bad. Fell off the jetway again.
jokes.setup: Lloyd and Harry reunite after their respective disasters; Harry casually asks how Lloyd's day was
jokes.punchline: 'Not bad. Fell off the jetway again.' — the word 'again' implies this is a recurring occurrence, delivered with total nonchalance
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The deadpan delivery of 'Fell off the jetway again' is a masterclass in comedic economy. The word 'again' does enormous work — it implies this has happened before, is not surprising, and is considered a 'not bad' day. The casualness of 'Hi, Lloyd / Hi, Harry' followed immediately by that revelation is structurally near-perfect. It earns 8.5+ on craft because the single word 'again' is brilliantly chosen and maximally funny for minimum words.

jokes.text: So you got fired again, huh? Oh, yeah. They always freak out when you leave the scene of an accident, you know?
jokes.setup: Harry deduces Lloyd was fired again from his driving job
jokes.punchline: Lloyd explains it matter-of-factly: employers 'always' freak out when you leave the scene of an accident — as if this is an unreasonable overreaction on their part
jokes.explanation: Excellent deadpan character comedy. 'They always freak out when you leave the scene of an accident' treats a serious crime as an inexplicable employer quirk. The word 'always' implies this has happened multiple times and Lloyd still doesn't understand why it's a problem. Great character voice and economy.

jokes.text: Yeah, well, I lost my job too. Man! You are one pathetic loser. No offense. No. None taken.
jokes.setup: Harry reveals he also lost his job
jokes.punchline: Lloyd calls Harry a 'pathetic loser' with apparent sincerity, then adds 'No offense' — with Harry genuinely taking none — despite Lloyd being in the same exact situation
jokes.explanation: The mutual obliviousness to their shared situation is perfectly captured here. Lloyd calling Harry a pathetic loser without any apparent self-awareness that he's in the same boat — and Harry accepting the insult graciously — is good buddy-comedy character work.

jokes.text: You know what really chaffs my ass, though? I spent my life's savings turning my van into a dog.
jokes.setup: Harry is lamenting his misfortunes after losing his job
jokes.punchline: His biggest grievance is that he spent his life savings converting a van into a giant dog shape — the Mutt Cutts van — revealing the depth of his financial and cognitive poor judgment
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Harry's major life investment was converting his van into a dog is a great absurdist character detail. 'Life's savings' applied to a novelty vehicle is a funny scale mismatch. 'What really chaffs my ass' as a lead-in sets up an expectation of a reasonable grievance, which makes the absurd truth funnier.

jokes.text: The alarm alone cost me 200. Hey! Chicks love it. It's a shaggin' wagon.
jokes.setup: Harry explains the financial outlay on his dog van
jokes.punchline: He defends the investment by noting 'chicks love it' and calling it a 'shaggin' wagon' — the idea of a dog-shaped van being a romantic vehicle is completely absurd but Harry is fully sold
jokes.explanation: Harry's delusion that the dog van is a romantic asset is a great character joke. 'Shaggin' wagon' applied to a vehicle shaped like a giant dog is an absurd non-sequitur delivered with complete confidence.

jokes.text: Man... I would have to be a lowlife to go rootin' around in somebody else's private property. Is it locked? Yeah, really well.
jokes.setup: Harry asks what's in the briefcase; Lloyd declares his moral high ground about not invading privacy
jokes.punchline: His very next words are asking if it's locked — immediately contradicting his stated principles, and Harry reporting it's 'really well' locked as the only obstacle
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured hypocrisy joke. The moral declaration followed immediately by the practical question exposes Lloyd's 'principles' as paper-thin. 'Yeah, really well' as Harry's response — treating lock quality as the only moral consideration — is a perfect button. Tight structure, good character integration, economical.

jokes.text: Harry: There's two of them. One of them's got a gun. [beat] Did you pay the gas bill?
jokes.setup: Harry spots two dangerous-looking men with guns approaching their apartment
jokes.punchline: His immediate follow-up to 'one of them's got a gun' is 'did you pay the gas bill?' — an utterly mundane non-sequitur that reveals their unfazed idiot logic
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic non-sequitur. The juxtaposition of 'one of them's got a gun' with 'did you pay the gas bill?' captures the characters' complete inability to prioritize correctly. The beat between the two lines is essential — the audience needs a half-second to register the threat before the mundane pivot lands. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: I don't think he's going to get that message, Joe. I mean, the guy's got worms in his living room.
jokes.setup: The villains are in Lloyd's apartment debating whether to trash it to send a message
jokes.punchline: One villain points out that someone who has worms in his living room is probably not going to register the trashed apartment as a meaningful threat — the character is already below any baseline of dignity
jokes.explanation: A smart joke that works as both a callback to the worm store detail and a villain's reasonable assessment of their target. The logic is sound — someone who keeps worms in their living room has different standards. Good economical delivery.

jokes.text: "I thought I taw a puddy cat. I did. I did." (squawks) (cracking)
jokes.setup: The villain decides to leave a 'better message' than trashing the apartment
jokes.punchline: He kills Lloyd's parakeet Petey by wringing its neck, quoting Tweety Bird mid-murder as dark comedic punctuation
jokes.explanation: A genuinely dark and original gag. Using Tweety Bird's catchphrase while snapping a parakeet's neck is an audacious piece of dark comedy — the juxtaposition of innocent cartoon reference and brutal action is both shocking and funny. The 'cracking' sound effect makes it land harder. This is Farrelly Brothers darkness at its best.

jokes.text: I can't believe we drove around all day and there's not a single job in this town. There is nothing, nada, zip! Yeah, unless you want to work 40 hours a week. Pfft!
jokes.setup: Lloyd and Harry lament the lack of job opportunities
jokes.punchline: Harry notes jobs exist — but only if you're willing to work 40 hours a week, which is apparently a disqualifying requirement; they treat full-time work as an unreasonable ask
jokes.explanation: A sharp observational/character joke. The 'Pfft!' reaction to 40-hour work weeks as an unreasonable imposition is both a great character beat and a broadly relatable absurdist sentiment. The structure is clean — the apparent complaint is false (there ARE jobs), but the heroes' standards eliminate them all.

jokes.text: Excuse me, little old lady. Uh, do you have change for a dollar? Change? No, I'm sorry. I don't. Oh... well, uh, could you do me a favor and watch my stuff here while I go break a dollar? Of course.
jokes.setup: Lloyd approaches an old lady on a motorized cart asking for change
jokes.punchline: When she can't make change, he asks her to watch his stuff — leaving his belongings with a stranger he just met for a trivially simple errand, also foreshadowing being robbed
jokes.explanation: A setup joke that earns its full payoff in the next beat. On its own, it's a mild character moment, but it functions as the first half of a well-constructed comic sequence. Lloyd's trust in a random stranger is very him.

jokes.text: Hey. I guess they're right. Senior citizens, although slow and dangerous behind the wheel, can still serve a purpose. I'll be right back. Don't you go dying on me!
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just asked the old lady to watch his stuff and she's agreed
jokes.punchline: He delivers a condescending 'they're right about seniors' speech, acknowledging they're 'slow and dangerous behind the wheel' but useful for guarding bags, then signs off with 'Don't you go dying on me!'
jokes.explanation: 'Don't you go dying on me!' is a great dark button. The whole speech is Lloyd being inadvertently offensive while thinking he's being magnanimous. 'Senior citizens, although slow and dangerous behind the wheel, can still serve a purpose' reads like Lloyd completing a thought he genuinely believes is a compliment.

jokes.text: I got robbed by a sweet old lady on a motorized cart. I didn't even see it coming.
jokes.setup: Lloyd had asked the old lady to watch his stuff and gone to make change
jokes.punchline: The old lady robbed him — 'I didn't even see it coming' implies he left his valuables with a stranger and is shocked at the outcome
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the setup joke lands well. 'I didn't even see it coming' is funny because of course he didn't — he left his stuff with a random person — but also because it implies even now he doesn't understand why it happened. The image of being robbed by a 'sweet old lady on a motorized cart' is inherently funny.

jokes.text: My parakeet Petey... Yeah? ...he's dead. (gasps) Aw... Oh, man. I'm sorry, Harry. What happened? His head fell off. His head fell off? Yeah, he was pretty old.
jokes.setup: Harry tells Lloyd his parakeet died; Lloyd expresses sympathy and asks what happened
jokes.punchline: 'His head fell off.' Then: 'Yeah, he was pretty old.' — Harry accepts this as a natural cause of death for an elderly bird, completely unaware the villains killed it
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire reel and arguably the film. 'His head fell off' as an explanation for death, accepted without question, is a masterpiece of deadpan character comedy. 'Yeah, he was pretty old' as the follow-up — treating decapitation as a natural consequence of avian aging — is brilliantly absurd. The dark layer (we know the villain killed the bird) adds a rewatch bonus. The two-man delivery, with Lloyd's 'His head fell off?' echo, is structurally perfect. This approaches the 9+ benchmark.

jokes.text: We got no food. We got no jobs. (yells) Our pets' heads are falling off!
jokes.setup: Lloyd is ranting about their terrible situation — no food, no jobs
jokes.punchline: He adds 'Our pets' heads are falling off!' as a third grievance, escalating from normal complaints to absurd horror, delivered at the same emotional pitch
jokes.explanation: A highly quotable escalation joke that works on multiple levels. The list structure (no food, no jobs, pets' heads falling off) uses the Rule of Three to devastating effect — the third item is an absurd escalation into horror that's delivered as an equal grievance. It's also a callback to Petey's death that reframes 'head fell off' as a broader pattern. This is genuine comedic writing craft: 'Our pets' heads are falling off!' has become one of the film's most quoted lines.

jokes.text: someplace warm... a place where the beer flows like wine, where beautiful women instinctively flock like the salmon of Capistrano. I'm talking about a little place called... Aspen.
jokes.setup: Lloyd is pitching Harry on leaving Providence for a dream destination
jokes.punchline: He builds up a Shangri-La fantasy — 'women flock like the salmon of Capistrano' — and reveals it's just Aspen, Colorado
jokes.explanation: 'Where beautiful women instinctively flock like the salmon of Capistrano' is a great absurdist image — mixing nature documentary language with romantic fantasy in a specifically wrong way. Salmon don't 'flock,' and Capistrano is famous for swallows not salmon. The whole speech treats Aspen like paradise while revealing Lloyd's delusional romantic worldview. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I don't know, Lloyd. The French are assholes.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just pitched Aspen as their destination
jokes.punchline: Harry's objection is that he doesn't know about going because 'the French are assholes' — Harry apparently believes Aspen is in France
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes and highly quotable. Harry's objection to Aspen — 'the French are assholes' — in six words reveals he thinks Aspen is in France (echoing Lloyd's 'California' mistake earlier), expresses a xenophobic non-sequitur as his primary concern, and treats his geographic ignorance as settled fact. Perfect economy, great character integration, and very funny on first watch and rewatch. This is comparable to the 8.0 benchmark anchor.

jokes.text: Wait a minute! I know what you're up to, mister. Yeah! You just wanna go to Aspen and find that girl who lost her briefcase, and you need me to drive you there! Right? Am I right? Am I right?
jokes.setup: Harry suspects Lloyd's ulterior motive for suggesting Aspen
jokes.punchline: Harry correctly identifies Lloyd's selfish motivation... but then goes to Aspen anyway, making the whole confrontation pointless
jokes.explanation: A functional character moment that sets up Harry's failed principled stand. The triple 'Am I right?' escalation is a good verbal tic but the joke itself is fairly standard buddy-movie fare.

jokes.text: Lloyd's crying as Harry agrees to Aspen — 'Okay okay, just let it out. Have a good cry.' then 'Okay. That's enough.'
jokes.setup: Harry agrees to go to Aspen; Lloyd is overcome with emotion
jokes.punchline: Harry coaches Lloyd through his crying, but then immediately cuts him off with 'Okay. That's enough.' — giving permission to emote, then revoking it
jokes.explanation: Harry's 'Okay. That's enough.' as the button to Lloyd's weeping is a good beat. The structured permission/revocation of emotional expression is a solid comedy mechanic. Relies on Carrey's physical commitment.

jokes.text: Lloyd, what are you doing? It feels like you're running at an incredible rate, Harry.
jokes.setup: They're on the road; Harry notices Lloyd is doing something in the car
jokes.punchline: Lloyd is apparently running in place (or doing some movement) in the passenger seat and reports it feels like he's 'running at an incredible rate' — presenting his self-delusion about physical activity with technical language
jokes.explanation: A compact absurdist character beat. Lloyd apparently exercises (or mimes exercising) in the passenger seat and reports a subjective sense of 'incredible rate' that obviously doesn't match reality. The specificity of 'incredible rate' makes it funnier than a vaguer description.

jokes.text: Would you quit it? We're not even through Connecticut yet, and already you're annoying me.
jokes.setup: Lloyd is doing something annoying in the passenger seat at the start of their cross-country road trip
jokes.punchline: Harry's complaint establishes they haven't even left Connecticut — implying the entire rest of the journey will be worse — delivered with weary resignation
jokes.explanation: A reliable road trip setup gag. 'Not even through Connecticut yet' efficiently establishes the scale of their journey and Harry's suffering. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Hey, where'd you get those? I bought them when we filled up. Well... We're supposed to talk about all expenditures, Lloyd. We're on a very tight budget.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has purchased something (ski goggles or similar accessory); Harry objects on budget grounds
jokes.punchline: The discovery of an unauthorized purchase on their 'very tight budget' — while they are embarking on a pointless cross-country road trip — is an ironic character beat about their completely wrong priorities
jokes.explanation: A setup moment more than a full joke — it establishes the financial tension that will pay off in the Petey reveal. On its own, it's functional character comedy about their delusional budget management.

jokes.text: No, I was able to raise 25 extra bucks before we left. Where did you get 25 extra bucks? I sold some stuff to Billy in 4C. The blind kid? Yeah! Yeah.
jokes.setup: Lloyd claims he raised extra travel money by selling 'stuff' to their neighbor, the blind kid
jokes.punchline: The confirmation that he sold things to a blind kid — who cannot assess what he's buying — is an immediately suspicious ethical red flag
jokes.explanation: A great setup for the Petey reveal. Harry's 'The blind kid? Yeah! Yeah.' — with Lloyd's emphatic agreement — perfectly sets up the horror of what was sold. The dark implication (selling to someone who can't see what they're buying) is well-structured.

jokes.text: What did you sell him, Lloyd? Stuff. What kind of stuff? I don't know. A few baseball cards, a sack of marbles... (coughs) Petey. Petey? You sold my dead bird to a blind kid? Lloyd, that-that... what are you... Petey didn't even have a head! Harry, I took care of it.
jokes.setup: Harry asks what Lloyd sold the blind kid; Lloyd hedges before the reveal
jokes.punchline: He sold Harry's headless dead bird to a blind child — with the escalating horror of 'Petey didn't even have a head!' met by Lloyd's breezy 'Harry, I took care of it.'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the reel and one of the film's signature moments. The escalating reveal structure is perfect: Lloyd hides the worst item until last (baseball cards, marbles... *cough* Petey), then Harry's escalating outrage ('You sold my DEAD bird to a BLIND kid?!', 'Petey didn't even have a HEAD!') builds beautifully, and Lloyd's completely calm 'Harry, I took care of it' as a response to selling a headless dead bird to a child is a transcendent piece of character comedy. This is the culmination of a multi-beat joke arc (Petey murdered → head fell off → sold to blind kid) and it fires on every cylinder. The payoff at '21:02' — 'Pretty bird' on the headless bird — adds another comedic layer.

jokes.text: Pretty bird. Yeah. Can you say, 'pretty bird'? Pretty bird. Yes, pretty bird. Pretty bird. Polly want a cracker?
jokes.setup: Lloyd told Harry he 'took care of it' regarding the headless dead bird sold to the blind kid
jokes.punchline: Cut to: Lloyd has apparently put something on the bird to make it look alive (inferred), and is coaching the blind child through 'talking' to it — 'Pretty bird... Polly want a cracker?' — the bird is headless and dead
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Lloyd 'selling' the headless dead bird by voicing it for the blind kid is a stunning piece of dark physical comedy. 'Pretty bird' repeated as if the bird is responding is simultaneously horrifying and hilarious. The layers of wrongness (dead, headless, sold to a child who can't see) make this one of the film's great dark comedy moments. Rewatch bonus is high because knowing the full Petey arc makes this even funnier.

jokes.text: Those rat bastards. They're rubbing it right in our faces.
jokes.setup: The villains see Harry and Lloyd driving away in the dog van
jokes.punchline: Joe interprets the dog van as a deliberate taunt — 'rubbing it right in our faces' — when it's simply Harry's idiotic van. The villains are projecting menace onto pure stupidity.
jokes.explanation: Smart comic irony — the villains interpret the dog van as sophisticated provocation when it's pure idiocy. The gap between the villain's perception of competent adversaries and the reality of Harry and Lloyd is a running source of comedy in the film.

jokes.text: Lloyd: They got The Monkees. They were a major influence on The Beatles. Yeah, I know.
jokes.setup: Lloyd and Harry are at a diner; Lloyd makes a musical observation
jokes.punchline: Lloyd states that The Monkees were a major influence on The Beatles — historically backwards (The Beatles came first) — and delivers it with complete confidence; Harry simply agrees
jokes.explanation: A compact ignorance joke that works on two levels: Lloyd's confident wrongness about music history, and Harry's agreement suggesting neither one has any idea. The casualness of delivery is key to the character.

jokes.text: Excuse me, Flo? (both laughing) Flo, like the TV show.
jokes.setup: Lloyd calls the waitress by what he assumes is her name, 'Flo'
jokes.punchline: He laughs at his own joke — that the waitress happens to be named like the TV show — suggesting this is a witty observation; both laugh as if this is clever rather than completely obvious
jokes.explanation: The joke is partly that Lloyd finds this observation funnier than it deserves — it's self-congratulatory humor from someone with low comedic standards. The character integration is solid but the joke itself is intentionally weak, which is the point.

jokes.text: Uh... what is the 'soup du jour'? It's the soup of the day. Mm-hmm... That sounds good. I'll have that.
jokes.setup: Lloyd asks the waitress to explain 'soup du jour' as if it's a specific proprietary item
jokes.punchline: When told it means 'soup of the day,' he treats this as a satisfying and meaningful answer — 'That sounds good. I'll have that.' — ordering the concept rather than knowing what the soup actually is
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-structured stupidity joke. The setup (not knowing what 'soup du jour' means) is common enough, but the specific punchline — being satisfied by the literal translation and ordering it without learning what the soup actually is — is a great character-specific extension. Lloyd is happy with the PHRASE 'soup of the day' as a sufficient answer. Very economical.

jokes.text: Anything else before I leave the area? No... yeah... yes yes, my soda's flat. It doesn't have any bubbles. (waiter blows bubbles into it) Happy now?
jokes.setup: Lloyd complains his soda is flat
jokes.punchline: The waitress resolves it by literally blowing through a straw into his soda, creating bubbles — a ridiculous 'fix' — then asks 'Happy now?' with apparent satisfaction
jokes.explanation: A great visual/physical gag. The waitress solving the flat soda problem by blowing into it (which is both gross and technically addresses the bubble complaint) is an absurdist solution delivered deadpan. 'Happy now?' as a satisfied button is well-timed.

jokes.text: Feels good to mingle with these laid-back country folk, don't it, Harr? I like it a lot.
jokes.setup: They're at a roadside diner; Lloyd surveys the patrons
jokes.punchline: He characterizes the clearly regional diner crowd as 'laid-back country folk' and expresses pleasure at 'mingling' with them — as if they're tourists observing an exotic culture rather than just two idiots at a diner
jokes.explanation: A mild observational character joke setting up the diner scene trouble. Lloyd's self-satisfied anthropological stance is in character but the joke doesn't do much more than establish his obliviousness.

jokes.text: You spilled the salt, that's what's the matter. Spilling the salt is very bad luck. We're driving across the country. The last thing we need is bad luck. Quick. Toss some salt over your right shoulder.
jokes.setup: Harry spills salt at the diner; Lloyd is alarmed
jokes.punchline: Lloyd lectures Harry about the bad luck of spilling salt in the context of their already-disastrous cross-country trip, then instructs him to throw salt over his shoulder — setting up the slapstick that follows
jokes.explanation: More of a setup than a standalone joke. The salt superstition lecture is functional, establishes Lloyd's credulous nature, and directly triggers the slapstick payoff. The irony of worrying about bad luck while already in a terrible situation is mild.

jokes.text: Harry throws salt over his shoulder directly into a biker's face. (thumps) Uh-oh, too little too late, Harry.
jokes.setup: Lloyd told Harry to throw salt over his shoulder for luck
jokes.punchline: Harry throws salt and immediately hits a large biker directly in the face; Lloyd's post-hoc verdict: 'too little too late'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed physical comedy payoff. The salt-to-biker's-face is a great immediate consequence for following superstitious advice, and 'too little too late, Harry' as Lloyd's verdict on the gesture — delivered after the damage is done — is a good ironic button.

jokes.text: Who's the dead man that hit me with the salt shaker?
jokes.setup: A large biker has been hit in the face with salt by Harry
jokes.punchline: He calls out 'Who's the dead man that hit me with the salt shaker?' — framing an accidental small incident as a capital offense, with the hyperbolic threat implicit in 'dead man'
jokes.explanation: A good threat line that works through hyperbolic menace applied to a trivial incident. 'Dead man' for a salt shaker incident is a funny escalation. Sets up the Sea Bass running gag.

jokes.text: Well... uh... it was a terrible mistake, sir. Please, believe me. I would never do anything to offend a man of your size.
jokes.setup: Sea Bass confronts Harry about the salt; Harry tries to apologize his way out
jokes.punchline: 'I would never do anything to offend a man of your size' — Harry's attempted compliment reveals he is specifically not afraid of offending small people, only large ones, which is both cowardly and inadvertently honest
jokes.explanation: 'A man of your size' is a great cringe-comedy line — it's meant to be flattery but reads as explicit size-based fear. The unintentional honesty of only respecting those who can physically intimidate you is a good character reveal for Harry.

jokes.text: You gonna eat that? What? That? No... yes... no. Well... no, it crossed my mind. Yeah. (snorts, hawks)
jokes.setup: Sea Bass is menacing Lloyd and Harry at the diner; instead of a threat, Sea Bass asks Lloyd about his food
jokes.punchline: The bizarre non-sequitur of 'You gonna eat that?' as an intimidation tactic, combined with Lloyd's confused hedging answer, then the hawking sound implying Sea Bass is about to spit in the food
jokes.explanation: The reel ends on this perfectly timed cringe moment. The unexpected pivot from physical threat to food question is a great misdirection; Lloyd's confused 'No... yes... no. Well... no, it crossed my mind' is classic cringe comedy. The ending hawk implies the spit gag and closes the reel on an appropriately escalating note.

jokes.text: Harry accuses Lloyd of wimping out for not eating the burger that the bully hawked on
jokes.setup: A bully just spat/hawked on Harry's burger as an act of intimidation
jokes.punchline: Harry calls Lloyd a wimp for not eating it, implying eating the defiled food would have been the brave choice — an absurd standard of toughness
jokes.explanation: Works because it's perfectly in character for Harry to have a completely skewed sense of machismo. The logic is idiotic and that's the point. Not a big laugh but a solid character beat.

jokes.text: Lloyd's scheming face — 'I think I just had an idea. Follow me.' — cutting to him apologetically approaching the bullies
jokes.setup: Lloyd dramatically declares he has a plan after the humiliating burger incident, building anticipation for some kind of revenge
jokes.punchline: His 'plan' opens with him meekly apologizing and offering to buy the bullies drinks — which looks like cowardly capitulation before the real scam is revealed
jokes.explanation: The two-stage misdirection works well: first we think Lloyd is caving, then we realize it's a con. Good structural comedy even if it's a familiar 'idiot-savant' beat.

jokes.text: Lloyd tells the waitress that 'Sea Bass and the fellas offered to pick up our check — they said just put it on their tab'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just privately promised the bullies free drinks; Harry is confused about how they can afford it
jokes.punchline: Lloyd has already pivoted to charging everything to the bullies' tab by fabricating their generosity to the waitress — the scam fully revealed
jokes.explanation: The punchline lands cleanly because the setup was doing double duty — Harry's confusion mirrored the audience's. The delivery of 'Sea Bass said that?' from the waitress adds a nice button. Well-structured comic payoff.

jokes.text: Sea Bass's reaction: 'I'm gonna kill those sons of bitches!' followed by Lloyd and Harry laughing hysterically in the car
jokes.setup: The scam has worked; Lloyd and Harry escape while Sea Bass is left with the bill
jokes.punchline: Sea Bass's explosive rage juxtaposed with the pair's gleeful laughter — the comedic release after the slow-burn con
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff beat. The rage vs. delight contrast is classic farce. Not original but executed with good energy.

jokes.text: Lloyd reveals the movie he copied the tab-scam from ended with the protagonist getting his throat slit half a mile down the road — 'It was a good one!'
jokes.setup: Harry praises the scam as genius and asks where Lloyd got the idea; Lloyd says he saw it in a movie, implying a clever caper
jokes.punchline: In the movie, the scammer was caught and murdered — Lloyd describes this as a great movie while apparently oblivious to the personal danger implication
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the reel. The structure is near-perfect: Harry's praise sets up an expectation of Lloyd crowing about cleverness; instead Lloyd reveals the movie ended in violent murder and finds it charming. The idiot-obliviousness is completely character-specific — Lloyd can't connect consequences to himself — and the dark turn is genuinely surprising. 'It was a good one!' as a button is the right level of economy. Approaches the 8-anchor quality.

jokes.text: Lloyd tells Harry to urinate into the empty beer bottles on the floor of the van rather than pull over
jokes.setup: Harry desperately needs to urinate while they're on the run; Lloyd refuses to pull over
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's completely practical solution is to pee into roadside beer bottles — gross and absurd but delivered as obvious common sense
jokes.explanation: Setup for a longer physical comedy sequence. The joke itself is mild but functional — it's the escalation that provides the real payoff.

jokes.text: Harry announces the bottle is almost full and he's still going; Lloyd tells him to 'just stop going' and Harry says 'I can't stop going once I've started — it stings'
jokes.setup: Harry is peeing into a beer bottle in the moving van; the bottle is nearly full
jokes.punchline: Harry is physically incapable of stopping mid-stream and treats this as a medical crisis, complete with the detail that stopping 'stings' — the absurdity of the bodily logistics treated with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the bottle crisis is well-paced. 'It stings' is a funny, specific, low-dignity detail. The chaos of Harry passing bottles while Lloyd drives adds physical comedy texture.

jokes.text: The bottle is almost full and Harry is 'still going' — he can't stop once he's started, 'it stings'
jokes.setup: Harry has been peeing into a beer bottle in the moving van
jokes.punchline: The bottle is overflowing and Harry physiologically cannot stop; the situation escalates to crisis
jokes.explanation: 'It stings' is a funny, specific, slightly TMI detail. The escalating panic over bottle capacity is good physical comedy even if it's broad. The 'can't stop once I've started' logic is absurdist and characterful.

jokes.text: Harry: 'What are you, a camel?' as the urination goes on and on requiring multiple bottles
jokes.setup: Harry has filled one beer bottle entirely and needed a second; the volume of urine is extraordinary
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's exasperated camel line — a simple but perfectly timed comic insult that reframes the gross-out as animal comedy
jokes.explanation: Economy is the strong suit here — three words that perfectly encapsulate the absurdity. Not the most original joke but it's the right line at the right moment.

jokes.text: Lloyd mishears the police siren's 'Pull over!' as a comment on his sweater — 'No, it's a cardigan, but thanks for noticing'
jokes.setup: A police siren blares 'Pull over!' at the van — a standard authoritative command
jokes.punchline: Lloyd hears it as a fashion observation and thanks the officer for the compliment on his cardigan — a perfect idiot mishearing that doubles as a pun
jokes.explanation: One of the great dumb-character jokes in mainstream comedy film. The wordplay is genuine ('pull over' the sweater vs. pull the vehicle over), it's perfectly in character — Lloyd's vanity and obliviousness are both on display simultaneously — and 'but thanks for noticing' is a genuinely charming button. The joke is tight, surprising, and entirely character-specific. Easily the standout joke of this reel and approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark, arguably surpassing it on character integration.

jokes.text: Following the cardigan mishear, Lloyd also compliments the officer: 'Killer boots, man!'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just confused 'pull over' with a sweater compliment; now a police officer approaches
jokes.punchline: Lloyd doubles down on the fashion-compliment frame by genuinely admiring the officer's boots — escalating the absurdity and showing no awareness of his peril
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback escalation. The cardigan line got the first big laugh; 'Killer boots, man!' extends the joke by showing Lloyd's entire interaction with authority has been filtered through fashion appreciation. Highly quotable and character-specific. The brevity is exactly right.

jokes.text: The officer spots what appears to be an open beer container (actually a bottle of Harry's urine) and demands it
jokes.setup: The officer has pulled them over suspecting drunk driving; he spots a bottle and assumes it's alcohol
jokes.punchline: The audience knows the bottle contains Harry's urine — the officer is about to drink pee while thinking he's confiscating alcohol
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the multi-bottle urine sequence. Classic dramatic irony — the audience is ahead of the officer and Lloyd/Harry's nervous protests ('No, sir, don't drink...') perfectly signal what's about to happen without over-explaining. The setup across several minutes earns this gross-out payoff.

jokes.text: Officer demands the bottle with 'Come on, give me that booze, you little pumpkin-pie-haircutted freak!'
jokes.setup: The officer is confiscating what he believes is alcohol from two apparent drunks
jokes.punchline: His insult — 'pumpkin-pie-haircutted freak' — is so specific, vivid and unhinged that it becomes funnier than any generic insult would be
jokes.explanation: The specific absurdity of 'pumpkin-pie-haircutted' is the joke — it's such a hyper-specific compound insult that it loops back around to funny. It's also a credible description of Lloyd's haircut. Good comic writing in the insult craft.

jokes.text: Harry offers the officer a Tic Tac immediately after the officer has swigged from the pee bottle
jokes.setup: The officer has just unknowingly drunk Harry's urine and is visibly reacting (coughing, retching)
jokes.punchline: Harry innocently offers a Tic Tac — the most absurdly understated response to the situation, implying the officer merely has bad breath rather than pee-mouth
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect button on the urine sequence. The Tic Tac offer is the ideal punchline: it's innocent, character-consistent (Harry is dim and well-meaning), absurdly understated given the gross reality, and it has perfect economy — two words do all the work. The officer's furious 'Get the hell outta here!' is the ideal reaction. This is the kind of joke that earns rewatch value because knowing it's coming makes the buildup funnier.

jokes.text: During the road-trip montage, someone tells a joke: 'So he says, do you love me? And she says, No, but that's a real nice ski mask'
jokes.setup: An intimate romantic question — 'do you love me?' — in what turns out to be a robbery context
jokes.punchline: She's responding to a robber, not a lover — the ski mask recontextualizes everything
jokes.explanation: A decent joke-within-the-movie. The misdirection works and it's snappy. Low character integration because it could be told by anyone, but it earns a solid chuckle as a road-trip gag.

jokes.text: During the road-trip montage, Harry audibly passes gas in the van
jokes.setup: Light-hearted road trip montage with music playing peacefully
jokes.punchline: An extended, clearly audible flatulence sound breaks the mood entirely
jokes.explanation: Straightforward gross-out gag with no particular setup or structure beyond the comedic contrast with the gentle music. Cheap but functional for its target audience. Below the episode's average craft level.

jokes.text: Lloyd's extended martial-arts fantasy daydream sequence — elaborate slow-motion fight choreography, battle cries, gurgling sound effects
jokes.setup: Lloyd is driving, apparently listening to music; we cut to an elaborate fantasy in which he's a skilled martial artist defeating opponents
jokes.punchline: The sequence becomes increasingly over-the-top — high-pitched battle cries, trilling, gurgling — before snapping back to reality. The gap between Lloyd's fantasy self-image and actual competence is the core joke
jokes.explanation: A sustained visual comedy set piece. The length is both the joke's strength (fully committing to the absurdity) and weakness (it slightly overstays). Lloyd's grandiose self-image expressed as an action hero fantasy is excellent character comedy. The sounds described in the transcript suggest escalating ridiculousness.

jokes.text: The van backfires dramatically; Harry asks 'You want me to drive?' and Lloyd says 'No, I'm cool'
jokes.setup: The van backfires with a loud bang, implying mechanical distress
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's breezy 'No, I'm cool' — delivered with total confidence despite the clearly struggling vehicle — is a perfect deadpan understatement
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective. 'I'm cool' is exactly the wrong thing to be in that moment and Lloyd's obliviousness is consistent character work. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'This is the life — cold beer, a hot tub and paper-thin walls' as they relax in the hot tub
jokes.setup: Lloyd and Harry are enjoying what they describe as 'the life' in what's clearly a low-budget motel hot tub
jokes.punchline: 'Paper-thin walls' as a luxury feature — Lloyd treats a hallmark of cheap motels as an amenity worth listing alongside beer and a hot tub
jokes.explanation: Nicely observed. The specificity of 'paper-thin walls' as the third listed luxury flips the audience's expectation and neatly characterizes these two as men with very low standards. Good economy.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'If you had a nice set of knockers' — the one thing that would make the hot tub moment better; Harry: 'That's two things, Lloyd'
jokes.setup: Lloyd says there's only one thing missing from their perfect moment
jokes.punchline: He specifies a 'nice set of knockers' — both crude and mathematically wrong since breasts are two things; Harry's correction ('That's two things, Lloyd') is the actual punchline
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: the crude wish and the perfectly logical correction. Harry's pedantry applied to something absurd is exactly the right comic move. The literalism is genuine character comedy — Harry isn't trying to be funny, he's just being precise.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'Yeah, well, it's a good thing you're not stacked, Harry, or I'd be banging you right now'
jokes.setup: Following the 'that's two things' correction, Lloyd escalates the hot-tub banter
jokes.punchline: Lloyd matter-of-factly states he would have sex with his best friend if he had breasts — delivered with complete sincerity and zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Lloyd's total lack of filter or social awareness is perfectly expressed here. The joke is earned by his character — it's not random shock, it's consistent with his obliviousness. The escalation from knockers to this is well-paced.

jokes.text: Lloyd continues: 'Split you like an old piece of firewood. You'd probably like it too, you big homo.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just said he'd sleep with Harry if he had breasts
jokes.punchline: He escalates to graphic specifics ('split you like old firewood') and then immediately calls Harry a 'homo' for supposedly enjoying it — the projection is complete and absurd
jokes.explanation: The projection humor (Lloyd is the one who brought up sex with Harry but calls Harry the homo) is funny in concept. 'Split you like old firewood' is a vivid, absurd image. The slur lands dated by modern standards and slightly undercuts the joke. Good escalation structure.

jokes.text: Harry describes his heartbreak over Fraida Felcher: 'right out of the blue, she sends me a John Deere letter'
jokes.setup: Harry is recounting a painful breakup with emotional sincerity — she sent him a 'Dear John' letter
jokes.punchline: He calls it a 'John Deere letter' — mixing up 'Dear John' with the farm equipment brand, and apparently has no idea he's said anything wrong
jokes.explanation: One of the best malapropism jokes in the film. The wordplay is genuine ('Dear John' / 'John Deere') and the error is completely in character — Harry is dumb enough to mix these up and sincere enough to never realize he has. The joke works on two levels: it's funny as a linguistic mistake and funny as a character revelation. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Matches the 8.0 benchmark anchor quality.

jokes.text: Harry explains his ex's reason for leaving: 'She gave me a bunch of crap about me not listening to her enough or something. I don't know. I wasn't really paying attention.'
jokes.setup: Harry is recounting Fraida's complaint that he didn't listen to her enough
jokes.punchline: 'I don't know. I wasn't really paying attention' — Harry unknowingly demonstrates the exact fault that ended his relationship in the act of describing it
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the reel. This is a perfect comedic construction: the setup and punchline are the same thing. Harry's inability to listen is DEMONSTRATED by his inability to listen while explaining his inability to listen. It's a closed loop of perfect ironic comedy. The delivery would need to be flat and sincere for it to fully land — Harry can't be in on the joke. It's deeply character-specific, economical, structurally elegant, and completely earned. This approaches the 9.5 anchor benchmark for Dumb and Dumber.

jokes.text: Lloyd's reaction to the mention of Fraida Felcher — 'Oh, yeah! I mean, I remember you... talking about her' — a suspicious overcorrection after initially sounding like he knew her personally
jokes.setup: Harry mentions his ex Fraida Felcher from Cranston; Lloyd immediately says 'Oh, yeah!' as if he knows her
jokes.punchline: Lloyd catches himself and awkwardly adds 'I mean, I remember you... talking about her' — a barely-covered slip that implies he knew Fraida Felcher more personally than he's letting on
jokes.explanation: A slow-burn plant joke — the audience picks up on the implication even if Harry doesn't. The overcorrection is played just right: enough to be suspicious without Lloyd explicitly confessing. Good character-based irony that pays off as subtext.

jokes.text: Harry looks at the map and announces: 'According to the map, we've only gone about four inches'
jokes.setup: They are calculating how much of their cross-country journey they've completed
jokes.punchline: Harry reports distance in literal map-inches rather than converting to miles — four inches on a US map means they've barely left their home state
jokes.explanation: Perfect idiot literalism. Harry cannot perform the basic conceptual step of converting map scale to real distance. The joke is clean and character-specific without being overworked.

jokes.text: Harry looks at the map: 'According to the map, we've only gone about four inches.'
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are driving cross-country and Harry is navigating
jokes.punchline: The 'four inches' on the map implies they've barely moved — taking the map scale literally
jokes.explanation: Classic idiot-navigator joke. The 'four inches' as a literal map measurement is a reasonable stupid-character mistake. Mildly amusing, well-placed.

jokes.text: Lloyd bets Harry he can get him gambling before end of day; Harry says 'I don't bet'; Lloyd offers 3-to-1, 5-to-1, 10-to-1 odds until Harry says 'You're on' — immediately losing the bet by accepting it
jokes.setup: Harry firmly declares he never gambles; Lloyd makes a bet that he can get Harry gambling, escalating the odds
jokes.punchline: Harry accepts the bet on 10-to-1 odds — in doing so, he has just gambled, losing the bet the instant he makes it
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever comedic construction. The escalating odds build real tension and the payoff is logically airtight — Harry loses the meta-bet the moment he accepts any bet. It's a classic trap joke with good pacing. The structure requires the audience to be slightly ahead of Harry, which gives it a satisfying 'click' when it lands. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Joe (the hitman) complains about wanting to kill Lloyd and Harry; his boss says 'You don't kill people you don't know. That's a rule.'
jokes.setup: Joe is eager to murder the two protagonists; his handler reins him in
jokes.punchline: The 'rule' against killing strangers is stated with the gravity of a professional ethics code — as if hitmen have a formal code of conduct that must be honored
jokes.explanation: Funny deadpan subversion — the professional ethics of murder framed as standard workplace policy. Dark comedy that works because it's delivered completely straight.

jokes.text: Lloyd and Harry pick up the hitman hitchhiker: 'We usually don't pick up hitchhikers, but I'm going to go with my instinct on this one. Saddle up, partner.'
jokes.setup: An armed hitman has been planted to get a ride and kill them; Lloyd is deciding whether to offer him a lift
jokes.punchline: Lloyd declares he's 'going with his instinct' — an instinct that is catastrophically wrong, since the hitchhiker is a killer. 'Saddle up, partner' adds a cheerful obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony does the heavy lifting — Lloyd's confidence in terrible judgment is perfectly in character. 'Saddle up, partner' is a nicely exuberant button.

jokes.text: Lloyd and Harry play an extended game of tag/quitsies/anti-quitsies/stamped-it in the front seat while the hitman looks on
jokes.setup: Two adults have just picked up a dangerous hitman; instead of normal conversation, they immediately devolve into a playground tag game with increasingly baroque rules
jokes.punchline: The hitman has to eventually yell 'Guys! Enough!' — the entire sequence played completely straight by Lloyd and Harry while a professional killer sits bewildered
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from multiple sources: the contrast of a hitman witnessing child behavior, the internal escalation logic of the tag rules ('you can't triple-stamp a double-stamp!'), and the sheer commitment of both actors. The hitman's exasperation is the perfect straight-man reaction. The chaos is funny precisely because Lloyd and Harry are completely in earnest.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'Hey, you wanna hear the most annoying sound in the world?' — followed by an extended screech directly at the hitman
jokes.setup: Following the tag chaos, things have barely settled; Lloyd immediately pivots to a new assault on everyone's nerves
jokes.punchline: Lloyd produces an extended, maximally irritating screech aimed at the hitman, who is trying to maintain composure while plotting to kill them
jokes.explanation: One of the most iconic moments in the film and arguably the most purely audience-participatory joke. The setup is a direct challenge to the audience ('wanna hear…') and the payoff is a full-commitment scream. The hitman's suffering amplifies the joke. Hugely quotable and extremely high-impact in a theater. The genius is that it's the audience who gets screeched at too.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'Radio? Who needs a radio?' — immediately launching into a full a cappella Mockingbird duet with Harry instead
jokes.setup: Mental asks for radio to get some relief from the chaos; Lloyd interprets this as an opportunity to perform
jokes.punchline: Lloyd and Harry launch into an enthusiastic (and presumably terrible) rendition, completely missing the point of Mental's request and making things worse
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'please let me have radio' to 'now they're SINGING at me' is perfectly logical for these characters. The commitment to performing the whole song only deepens the hitman's torment. Good sustained cringe-escalation.

jokes.text: Harry spots some people wanting a ride — reveals them to be cows — 'Pick 'em up!'
jokes.setup: Harry looks out the window and says there are people who want a ride too
jokes.punchline: They are cows. Harry cannot distinguish between roadside cows and hitchhiking humans
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist beat. Harry's animal-blindness is consistent with his general stupidity. 'Pick 'em up!' adds the right note of enthusiasm. Brief but lands.

jokes.text: Harry offers Mental an 'atomic pepper' and when Mental declines, the two argue in childlike fashion about who goes first eating one
jokes.setup: In a roadside diner, Harry offers Mental a novelty hot pepper; Mental declines; Lloyd and Harry then dare each other to eat one
jokes.punchline: The daring sequence is entirely childish ('you go first / no you go first / I always go first') while a hitman watches and eventually loses patience
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat that sets up the pepper payoff. The back-and-forth daring is familiar comedy territory but executed with appropriate energy.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd eat atomic peppers; first claim 'it's more tingly than hot' then immediately erupt in screaming and gagging
jokes.setup: Both eat an 'atomic pepper' and bravely maintain it's not so bad
jokes.punchline: The delayed reaction — brief false bravado followed by an explosive meltdown — is perfectly timed physical comedy
jokes.explanation: The brief beat of false bravado ('it's more tingly than hot') before collapse is well-structured. A classic delayed reaction joke. Physical comedy plays well and the screaming/gagging escalation is fully committed.

jokes.text: Mental excuses himself to use the phone — 'Enjoy your meal, guys' — leaving two grown men whimpering over peppers
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are screaming and gagging from the peppers; Mental is trying to call in an update to his boss
jokes.punchline: His polite 'enjoy your meal' exit line, delivered to two writhing men, is a perfect deadpan social grace in an absurd context
jokes.explanation: Mental's deadpan politeness as a running characterization works here. 'Enjoy your meal' to two people in agony is the right absurdist social nicety. Good economy.

jokes.text: Mental calls his boss from the diner and announces he'll 'dump a little rat poison in their Shirley Temple'
jokes.setup: Mental checks in with his boss about eliminating Lloyd and Harry
jokes.punchline: His murder method is rat poison in a Shirley Temple — the most child-associated cocktail imaginable, perfectly matched to the two man-children he's trying to kill
jokes.explanation: The 'Shirley Temple' detail is the genius of this joke. It's not just any drink — it's the non-alcoholic child's drink, which perfectly characterizes Lloyd and Harry without having to say so. Dark comedy that works because the detail is specific and apt.

jokes.text: Harry offers Mental: 'Here, Lloyd, this helps!' — pressing milk/remedy to Lloyd's burning mouth while whimpering — and when Lloyd uses it, says 'It works good'
jokes.setup: Both are suffering from atomic peppers; Harry discovers a remedy
jokes.punchline: Their shared suffering and mutual self-treatment while a hitman eats calmly nearby; 'It works good' is a nicely undignified button
jokes.explanation: Functional coda to the pepper bit. Not particularly inventive but the contrast of their suffering against Mental's calm is consistent and mildly amusing. Below average for the reel.

jokes.text: Mental asks why they're going to Aspen; Harry says 'Why don't you eat up and we'll tell you?' with Lloyd — both still whimpering — snorting at their own feeble attempt at wit
jokes.setup: Mental asks a reasonable question; Harry attempts to be coy and witty while still suffering from pepper burns
jokes.punchline: Both crack up at Harry's weak non-answer as if it were brilliantly clever — their self-satisfaction is the joke
jokes.explanation: Their mutual admiration for their own mediocre quip is good character work. Not a big laugh but authentic to both characters.

jokes.text: Harry casually tells Mental the briefcase isn't theirs — some lady left it at the airport, they're just returning it — without realizing this is the information that will get them killed
jokes.setup: Mental has been trying to discover what the two know about the briefcase; Harry volunteers the entire story without prompting
jokes.punchline: Mental laughs — genuinely appalled by the irony that two completely innocent idiots have waltzed into a kidnapping ransom situation. The audience shares his disbelief
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony peaks here — Mental's laugh of disbelief is the audience surrogate reaction. Harry's total innocence and openness is what makes Lloyd and Harry simultaneously dangerous and untouchable. Good plot-integrated comedy.

jokes.text: Mental doubles over groaning — the rat poison he intended for them has somehow ended up poisoning him instead
jokes.setup: Mental announced he would poison their Shirley Temples with rat poison; we next see him in agony
jokes.punchline: The implied reversal — the assassin has been poisoned, presumably by getting his own poison mixed up or somehow consuming it himself — karma delivered as physical comedy
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff to the rat poison setup is enormously satisfying. The implication without explicit explanation is the right choice — the audience fills in the gap. The irony of a hitman being hoisted by his own petard is a classic comic structure executed efficiently.

jokes.text: Lloyd attempts CPR on the poisoned hitman — 'Don't worry. I know CPR.' — then proceeds to visibly do it wrong while Mental screams 'Get off!'
jokes.setup: Mental needs medical help; Lloyd volunteers with supreme confidence
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's CPR is clearly wrong (described through Mental's screaming resistance and Lloyd's narration 'out with the bad air, in with the good'), performed with total misplaced confidence
jokes.explanation: Classic incompetent-helper comedy. Lloyd's confidence in his ability to perform CPR is funnier than any explicit demonstration of error. 'Out with the bad air, in with the good' is a nicely wrong mnemonic. The hitman resisting being saved by the people he was trying to kill adds an extra layer.

jokes.text: After giving Mental his pills, Lloyd asks: 'You want some ketchup and mustard? That helped us.' — referencing the atomic pepper remedy
jokes.setup: Mental has just received his emergency pills; Lloyd wants to help further
jokes.punchline: Lloyd offers condiments as a remedy for poisoning, based on his and Harry's experience with hot peppers — a completely false equivalence delivered with earnest helpfulness
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback that works because the false equivalence (pepper burn = rat poisoning) is exactly how Lloyd's brain works. 'That helped us' is delivered with complete sincerity. The absurdist logic is consistent with the character. Good economy and a satisfying button on the diner sequence.

jokes.text: Mental's final 'Son of a bitch!' (gurgling) as the scene ends — his last reaction to Lloyd and Harry's 'help'
jokes.setup: Mental has been poisoned, subjected to amateur CPR, and offered condiments as medicine
jokes.punchline: His final gurgled curse is both an expression of physical agony and total exasperation — a hitman defeated not by skill but by sheer idiocy
jokes.explanation: A satisfying button on the whole Mental sequence. The gurgling adds the right physical comedy detail. His defeat via incompetent kindness is thematically consistent with the film's whole ethos.

jokes.text: Life's a fragile thing, Harr. One minute you're chewing on a burger, the next minute you're dead meat.
jokes.setup: A man has just died — Lloyd reflects on the fragility of life with apparent sincerity
jokes.punchline: "dead meat" lands as an unintentional (to Lloyd) pun about the burger, reducing a man's death to a deli metaphor
jokes.explanation: The pun is accidental from Lloyd's perspective, which is what makes it work — his obliviousness is the joke. 'Dead meat' perfectly doubles as literal food commentary and metaphor for death. Clean character integration: only a lovable idiot delivers a eulogy this way.

jokes.text: Those were his last words. / Not if you count the gurgling sound.
jokes.setup: Harry laments that the dying man blamed him — 'those were his last words'
jokes.punchline: Lloyd matter-of-factly corrects the record: technically the death rattle came after
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and structure. The setup frames 'last words' as a solemn, finalistic statement; Lloyd punctures it with clinical pedantry about the gurgling noise. It's dark, perfectly timed, and totally in character for Lloyd's oblivious literal-mindedness. One of the reel's strongest lines — the specificity of 'the gurgling sound' elevates it above generic dark humor.

jokes.text: They're driving an '84... sheepdog.
jokes.setup: Investigators are tracking the suspects and ask for a make on their vehicle — standard police procedural beat
jokes.punchline: The officer deadpans that the vehicle is an '84 sheepdog — a callback to the van shaped like a giant dog from earlier in the film
jokes.explanation: The delivery in the register of a straight police report — model year and all — applied to an absurd dog-shaped van is a perfect deadpan. The pause before 'sheepdog' and the year-make format sell it. Strong rewatch bonus because knowing the van makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Both of 'em? / Yeah. / Cool.
jokes.setup: Harry is making small talk with a female hitchhiker about her skis, asking if they're hers
jokes.punchline: His follow-up 'both of 'em?' is a spectacularly stupid question — skis come in pairs — and his satisfied 'Cool' after her confirmation reveals he thought this was profound
jokes.explanation: Pure character comedy. The question 'both of 'em?' is so genuinely stupid — there is no other number of skis — that it perfectly encapsulates Harry's dim worldview. His self-satisfied 'Cool' at the confirmation makes it land harder. Very lean, no wasted words.

jokes.text: Harry awkwardly asking a woman at a gas station whether both skis are hers, stretching the conversation to absurd length.
jokes.setup: Harry spots an attractive woman with skis and attempts conversation. The dialogue exchange — 'Skis, huh?' / 'Both of 'em?' / 'Cool.' — is painfully thin.
jokes.punchline: The cumulative awkwardness of his attempts to extend a conversation with absolutely nothing to say; the interaction dies on 'Cool.'
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy of a socially inept man failing spectacularly at small talk. The escalating inanity of each question is the joke. Functional but not memorable.

jokes.text: Um, excuse me, but you're, uh... you're spraying everywhere.
jokes.setup: Harry has stopped to use a roadside urinal while the hitchhiker waits; she politely informs him he's making a mess
jokes.punchline: Harry's oblivious whistling continues mid-stream — the visual and audio of a grown man cheerfully urinating all over himself and the surroundings while someone watches is the gag
jokes.explanation: Functional gross-out physical comedy. The whistling detail adds a layer of cheerful obliviousness that elevates it slightly above pure toilet humor, but it's not especially novel.

jokes.text: That's a lot of luggage for a little vacation.
jokes.setup: Mental spots Harry's large amount of luggage loaded on the vehicle
jokes.punchline: The line is delivered as idle menacing small talk by a terrifying trucker — the mundanity of the observation against the terror of the speaker is the comic contrast
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh from the contrast of threatening figure making banal chit-chat. Not a strong joke on its own but serves the scene's rhythm.

jokes.text: Harry tries to help the hitchhiker with her ski boot buckle, then accidentally ignites gasoline with a lighter
jokes.setup: Harry helpfully offers to fix the hitchhiker's loose ski boot, fumbles with his lighter
jokes.punchline: He ignites something — the visual gag of his bumbling helpfulness literally causing a fire
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that earns its laugh from Harry's earnest desire to help compounded by catastrophic incompetence. The escalation from boot-fixing to fire is well-structured visually.

jokes.text: Sure. You know, I'm heading up to Aspen myself. Maybe we could, you know, meet up, have some hot chocolate or something.
jokes.setup: Harry has just accidentally set something on fire while trying to help; he pivots immediately to casual flirting
jokes.punchline: The breezy 'hot chocolate or something' invite, delivered as if nothing catastrophic just happened, is the joke
jokes.explanation: Harry's total compartmentalization of disaster into opportunity is consistent character comedy. 'Hot chocolate or something' is comically understated as a romantic pitch moments after causing a fire.

jokes.text: The number's 555... 905... wait a minute. That's my old number. That is so weird how your mind just goes blank.
jokes.setup: Harry is eager to get the hitchhiker's phone number and suggests he memorize it
jokes.punchline: She recites the wrong number, then trails into a confused non-explanation — the joke is that this supposedly simple task collapses immediately
jokes.explanation: Mild observational comedy about memory failure. Functional but not particularly sharp — the joke is familiar and the character (the hitchhiker) isn't the film's comedic engine.

jokes.text: For God's sakes, just give me the damn number! / Okay, look, uh, you gonna get pushy, forget about it.
jokes.setup: Harry has been patiently waiting through the hitchhiker's memory failure and finally snaps
jokes.punchline: The hitchhiker immediately revokes the offer because Harry got 'pushy' — after she was the one causing the delay
jokes.explanation: Good comic reversal: Harry's entirely justified frustration is used against him by the person who was wasting his time. The injustice of it is the laugh.

jokes.text: Find a happy place. Find a happy place. Find a happy place. / I'll show you a happy place.
jokes.setup: Harry is trying to calm himself down with a self-help mantra while Mental looms nearby
jokes.punchline: Mental's sinister response 'I'll show you a happy place' — implying violence — subverts the soothing context of the mantra completely
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of gentle self-help language with a large threatening man is well-executed. 'I'll show you a happy place' works on multiple levels — the flat sinister delivery against the warm phrase makes it darkly funny. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: I promise not to mention another word about you being in a bathroom with a 6'4" trucker with his pants down.
jokes.setup: Lloyd tells Harry to drop whatever happened; Harry says fine, he promises not to bring it up
jokes.punchline: Lloyd immediately describes the entire humiliating incident in graphic detail as his version of 'not mentioning it'
jokes.explanation: Classic comic irony structure: 'I promise not to mention X' followed immediately by a detailed account of X. The specific detail — '6'4" trucker with his pants down' — is perfectly chosen to maximize Harry's humiliation while giving Lloyd maximum plausible deniability. Strong character integration: Lloyd is not being cruel, just oblivious.

jokes.text: Hey, look. We're almost in Colorado. What do you say we change seats? I've been driving for nine straight hours. / I don't have the energy to start a new state.
jokes.setup: Harry reasonably requests a driving swap after nine straight hours
