jokes.punchline: Lloyd refuses on the grounds that he doesn't have the energy 'to start a new state' — as if state lines require renewed emotional commitment
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever character-specific absurdism. 'Start a new state' treats a geographic line as an emotional threshold requiring psychic preparation. It's a funny concept delivered with Lloyd's signature exhausted self-pity. High character integration — this logic belongs to Lloyd alone.

jokes.text: Why should I do you any favors? / I'll let you kiss me.
jokes.setup: Lloyd asks why he should give Harry a favor (the driving swap)
jokes.punchline: Harry offers to let Lloyd kiss him as the incentive — a grotesque non-reward framed as a gift
jokes.explanation: Harry's total obliviousness to social norms — offering himself as a romantic prize to his male friend as if it's a reasonable transaction — is good character comedy. The confidence of the offer is the joke.

jokes.text: Harry slaps and wrestles with Lloyd while driving, and Lloyd retaliates with the same mocking whine
jokes.setup: Harry threatens to 'take' something from Lloyd (escalating argument in the car)
jokes.punchline: The threat devolves into petulant slapping and 'don't touch me' squabbling — two grown men acting like children on a highway
jokes.explanation: Standard buddy-comedy bickering. Functional physical comedy but not particularly original. The infantile quality fits the characters but doesn't rise above the expected.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. Whoa, Big Gulps, huh? All right. Well, see you later.
jokes.setup: Lloyd pulls into a gas station; we see (from dialogue) people there with large drinks
jokes.punchline: Lloyd offers a completely non-sequitur observation about their drinks, gets nothing in return, and immediately says 'see you later' as if this was a complete social interaction
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes and arguably one of the film's most iconic moments. The structure is perfect: Lloyd initiates a social exchange with a meaningless observation, receives zero response, and immediately closes the loop with 'see you later' — treating the whole non-interaction as satisfying. It's absurdist, deeply character-specific, economical to the extreme, and completely baffling in the best way. The joke has legs: it's been quoted for thirty years because it encapsulates the film's spirit in nine words. Earns the high score.

jokes.text: Some people just weren't cut out for life on the road.
jokes.setup: Harry has fallen asleep in the passenger seat; Lloyd looks over at his snoring friend
jokes.punchline: Lloyd delivers a wistful, sage-like pronouncement about road life for someone who is simply asleep after a long drive
jokes.explanation: Lloyd's grandiose self-positioning as a veteran of the road when they've been driving for one day is funny. The delivery — melancholy wisdom — against the mundane reality (Harry took a nap) is a good deadpan.

jokes.text: I expected the Rocky Mountains to be a little rockier than this. / I was thinking the same thing. / That John Denver's full of shit, man.
jokes.setup: They are driving through flat terrain — apparently nowhere near the Rockies — having expected mountains based on the song 'Rocky Mountain High'
jokes.punchline: Their shared disappointment culminates in Lloyd blaming John Denver by name as if he personally misled them
jokes.explanation: A legitimately excellent joke. The setup — two idiots expecting geography to match a pop song — is perfect character comedy. The escalation from disappointment to Harry's straight-man agreement to Lloyd's flat, furious verdict on John Denver is impeccably structured. 'Full of shit, man' is delivered with genuine grievance, as if Denver has personally wronged them. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, economically perfect. Earns a high score.

jokes.text: So we backtracked a tad! / A tad?! A tad, Lloyd? You drove almost 1/6 of the way across the country in the wrong direction!
jokes.setup: Lloyd has driven them significantly in the wrong direction; he minimizes it as a 'tad'
jokes.punchline: Harry's precise calculation — '1/6 of the way across the country' — contrasted with Lloyd's 'tad' reveals the scale of the blunder
jokes.explanation: The mathematical precision of '1/6 of the way across the country' against 'a tad' is the joke. Harry's incredulity is well-earned. Solid escalation comedy.

jokes.text: Now we don't have enough money to get to Aspen! We don't have enough money to get home! We don't have enough money to eat! We don't have enough money to sleep!
jokes.setup: Harry itemizes their financial catastrophe after Lloyd's wrong-direction detour
jokes.punchline: The escalating list — from mission-critical (get to Aspen) down to basic survival needs (sleep) — reveals just how comprehensively they've ruined themselves
jokes.explanation: The list joke works through escalation — going from the goal to basic survival needs is a good structure — but it's a fairly standard 'everything is terrible' comedy beat. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: It's not gonna do us any good to sit here whining about it. We're in a hole. We're just going to have to dig ourselves out.
jokes.setup: Lloyd, who caused all of the problems, now delivers a motivational speech
jokes.punchline: The irony that the person who drove them into a catastrophe is now dispensing wisdom about digging out of holes — with apparent sincerity and self-awareness — is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good ironic character moment. Lloyd's total lack of self-awareness in pivoting to leadership mode is consistent with his character. 'We're in a hole' has mild unintentional irony given he dug it.

jokes.text: Oh, well, pardon me, Mr. Perfect! I guess I forgot that you never, ever make a mistake!
jokes.setup: Harry decides to walk home in disgust; Lloyd calls after him
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's sarcastic 'Mr. Perfect' defense — implying Harry is being a hypocrite — is funny because Harry is also an idiot, but in this instance was not at fault
jokes.explanation: Standard defensive-idiot comedy. Gets the job done as Lloyd's character moment but isn't a particularly inventive line.

jokes.text: Engine backfire startles Lloyd — he screams
jokes.setup: Lloyd has been chasing Harry down the road; a vehicle backfires
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's outsized scream at a mundane noise, mid-chase, punctuates the slapstick escalation
jokes.explanation: Basic slapstick beat. The timing works in context but it's a cheap laugh off a stock comedic device.

jokes.text: I can get 70 miles to the gallon on this hog.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just revealed he traded a van for a tiny moped/minibike
jokes.punchline: He calls the tiny vehicle a 'hog' — biker slang for a large motorcycle — and quotes fuel efficiency as if this is a sophisticated vehicular choice
jokes.explanation: Calling a child's minibike a 'hog' is funny on its own, but adding the specific fuel efficiency stat ('70 miles to the gallon') with total pride transforms it into a great line. Lloyd's earnest salesmanship of an objectively terrible decision is pitch-perfect character comedy. The contrast between 'hog' (Harley-Davidson connotations) and the actual vehicle is a compact, well-constructed visual/dialogue joke. Near-anchor-level economy and character integration.

jokes.text: You know, Lloyd, just when I think you couldn't possibly be any dumber, you go and do something like this... and totally redeem yourself!
jokes.setup: Harry begins what sounds like a familiar insult — 'just when I think you couldn't possibly be any dumber...'
jokes.punchline: The expected conclusion ('...you go and prove me wrong') is replaced with '...and totally redeem yourself!' — Harry finds the moped genuinely impressive
jokes.explanation: One of the great misdirection jokes in the film. The setup perfectly imitates a classic insult structure that the audience — and Harry — has probably delivered before, so the pivot to 'totally redeem yourself' lands as a genuine surprise. It's a double joke: funny on first viewing as misdirection, funnier on rewatch because Harry's sincere admiration for the moped is itself absurd. The specific pause between the two halves — written into the structure — is crucial. Highly quotable, widely remembered, strong enough to anchor any reel. Earns the high score.

jokes.text: Still wanna go to Aspen? / Oh, yeah! / Okay, let's go, buddy! / Super! / Lloyd, no! West! Go west, Lloyd! / Oh! Oh, yeah.
jokes.setup: They excitedly mount the moped and take off for Aspen
jokes.punchline: Lloyd immediately heads in the wrong direction again — east instead of west — requiring Harry to correct him
jokes.explanation: A quick callback to the wrong-direction mistake that lands because it comes immediately after their triumphant new start. Lloyd's chipper 'Oh! Oh, yeah' — no shame, no embarrassment — is perfect. The timing is fast enough that it doesn't overstay.

jokes.text: I've got to... I've got to stop to go to the bathroom. / Just go, man.
jokes.setup: Harry needs to use the bathroom while they're riding the moped — there's nowhere to stop
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's casual 'just go, man' — implying Harry should urinate while riding — followed by Harry apparently complying ('Oh! That sure is warm.')
jokes.explanation: The 'just go, man' advice combined with Harry's reaction ('That sure is warm') confirms the gross-out without over-explaining it. The economy is excellent — the whole bit is three lines. The warmth observation is perfectly stupid and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Oh! That sure is warm.
jokes.setup: Harry is riding on the back of a moped and has just relieved himself while moving, per Lloyd's advice
jokes.punchline: His only observation is a contented 'That sure is warm' — treating the disgusting situation as mildly pleasant
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that do enormous comedic work. The warmth observation is both a logical consequence (of course it's warm) and a completely wrong emotional register for the situation. Harry's equanimity in disgusting circumstances is a core character trait, and this line is one of its purest expressions. The understatement is the craft.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd arrive in Aspen visibly frozen after riding a moped through mountain passes
jokes.setup: They set off on a child's moped through the Rocky Mountains, optimistic
jokes.punchline: They arrive in Aspen as shivering, frozen wrecks — the visual consequence of their baffling vehicle choice
jokes.explanation: Visual payoff to the moped sequence. The frozen shivering is an earned consequence and the visual of two men huddled on a tiny moped in the Rockies is funny. Not a joke on its own — more a satisfying physical punctuation mark.

jokes.text: Got a little nippy going through the pass back there.
jokes.setup: They have just arrived in Aspen visibly hypothermic after riding a moped through a mountain pass
jokes.punchline: Harry describes near-freezing on a mountain pass as 'a little nippy'
jokes.explanation: Classic British-style understatement applied to an American idiot. 'A little nippy' for near-hypothermia is a clean, economical deadpan. The character-specific obliviousness makes it work.

jokes.text: Ho... Jeez, look at the butt on that. / Yeah. He must work out.
jokes.setup: Harry spots an attractive person and comments on their physique; the audience (and Lloyd) expects him to be talking about a woman
jokes.punchline: Lloyd confirms it's a man ('he must work out') — both are admiring a man's rear end without any self-consciousness
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the first line sets up an expectation the film plays straight, then the gender reveal is the punchline. Their shared, completely unselfconscious admiration of a man's physique is funny because it's played purely straight. Economical and effective.

jokes.text: If I know her as well as I think I do, she'll invite us right in for tea and strumpets.
jokes.setup: Lloyd confidently predicts Mary will welcome them warmly
jokes.punchline: He says 'strumpets' instead of 'crumpets' — a strumpet being an archaic word for a promiscuous woman — without any awareness of the malapropism
jokes.explanation: A malapropism that works on two levels: it's a natural idiot mistake (strumpets/crumpets sound similar) AND it accidentally implies something about Mary that is unintentionally inappropriate given Lloyd's supposed romantic reverence for her. The double-layer gives it more craft than a typical dumb-character word error. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Starts with an 'S.' S-swim, Swamie, S-slippy, Slappy, Slimin, Solmon, Simin, Sal, Swenson, Swanson?
jokes.setup: Harry asks Mary's last name so they can look her up; Lloyd doesn't know it
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's frantic stream-of-consciousness guessing — a cascade of wrong names with escalating desperation — reveals he went cross-country for a woman whose name he doesn't know
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of wrong names is well-performed physical comedy (the rapid-fire delivery is half the joke). The underlying absurdity — the entire journey's premise collapses because he doesn't know her last name — gives the moment weight beyond the gag itself.

jokes.text: Maybe it's on the briefcase. / Oh, yeah! It's right here. / Samsonite! I was way off.
jokes.setup: They consider looking up the name; Harry suggests checking the briefcase
jokes.punchline: Lloyd triumphantly reads 'Samsonite' — the brand name of the briefcase — and concludes it's her last name. His 'I was way off' self-assessment while being completely wrong is the kicker
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best stupidity jokes. The logic is internally consistent for an idiot: the briefcase has a name on it, the name must belong to its owner. 'Samsonite!' delivered as a breakthrough revelation is perfect. But 'I was way off' is the masterstroke — it implies Lloyd recognizes the gap between his guesses and 'Samsonite' as a similarity problem rather than a category error. His self-criticism is precisely wrong in the funniest way. Economical, character-perfect, highly quotable.

jokes.text: Ooh. Maybe you should wear these extra gloves. My hands are starting to get sweaty. / Extra gloves? You've had this pair of extra gloves this whole time?
jokes.setup: Harry has been freezing and complaining his fingers are numb after the moped journey
jokes.punchline: Lloyd casually produces extra gloves he has had the entire time and only now offers them because his own hands are sweaty
jokes.explanation: The reveal is perfectly timed. Lloyd's motivation for sharing — not empathy but sweaty hands — is a sharp character detail. His casual 'we're in the Rockies' justification for bringing extra gloves implies he planned ahead for himself and simply never thought to mention it. Harry's disbelieving repetition of 'this whole time' is the audience's reaction voiced. Well-structured surprise.

jokes.text: Harry's fingers are numb from the cold — Lloyd produces a pair of extra gloves he has been carrying the entire time.
jokes.setup: Harry has been complaining about frozen fingers for some time.
jokes.punchline: Lloyd casually produces extra gloves he's had in his pocket the whole time — 'Yeah. We're in the Rockies.' — as though this was obvious planning.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Lloyd's casual explanation — 'We're in the Rockies' — implying that of course you pack extra gloves, while he never thought to offer them when Harry was suffering. The oblivious selfishness is perfectly in character, and Harry's murderous reaction ('I'm going to kill you') is well-earned. 'My hands are starting to get sweaty' as the trigger is a great detail.

jokes.text: I'm going to kill you. / What? / I'm gonna kill you! I'm gonna kill you, Lloyd! / Calm down! / Right now, I'm gonna kill you!
jokes.setup: Harry discovers Lloyd had extra gloves the whole time he was suffering from the cold
jokes.punchline: Harry's repeated murder threats — escalating in specificity and urgency — delivered to Lloyd's baffled calm, play the disproportionate rage against Lloyd's obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation beat. The repeated 'I'm gonna kill you' works as a payoff to the glove frustration, but it's fairly standard comedic rage. Lloyd's calm in the face of it is funnier than the threats themselves.

jokes.text: We'll borrow a few bucks from the briefcase and keep track with IOUs. We'll be meticulous, right down to the last penny. Whatever we borrow, we pay back. Our word is our bond.
jokes.setup: Penniless in Aspen, Lloyd proposes a plan to borrow from the ransom briefcase
jokes.punchline: The elaborate ethical framework — IOUs, meticulous accounting, 'our word is our bond' — applied to stealing from a ransom case by two men who can barely navigate a road is an ironic masterpiece of self-delusion
jokes.explanation: The gap between their solemn ethical code ('our word is our bond') and what they're actually doing (robbing a ransom briefcase) is well-played. Both characters buying into the honor-system framing equally is funnier than if one were more skeptical.

jokes.text: Presidential Suite speech: '...normally reserved for royalty, visiting dignitaries, illustrious stars of stage and screen... Emperor and Empress of Japan, and of course Princess Charles and Di...' / We'll take it!
jokes.setup: A hotel concierge describes the Presidential Suite in grandiose terms to two penniless men who just broke into a ransom briefcase
jokes.punchline: Lloyd cuts off the speech with an enthusiastic 'We'll take it!' — no consideration of cost, entirely confident, based on nothing
jokes.explanation: Bonus absurdity from 'Princess Charles' — a malapropism for Prince Charles. The 'We'll take it!' interrupt is a satisfying payoff: they've been catastrophically poor for ten minutes and now they're renting the presidential suite. Good escalation of their absurd spending.

jokes.text: Princess Charles and Di when they were together used to frequent the hotel constantly.
jokes.setup: The concierge name-drops celebrity guests
jokes.punchline: 'Princess Charles' — apparently the concierge means Prince Charles — is a small but funny misgendering of royalty, possibly intentional camp
jokes.explanation: Minor joke embedded in the Presidential Suite scene. 'Princess Charles' is funny as an error that reveals the concierge may not be as classy as the room. Small but landed.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd sobbing together watching a sentimental phone company TV commercial
jokes.setup: They are in the presidential suite watching TV — a TV advertisement for Pacific Bell plays
jokes.punchline: Both are openly weeping at a phone company commercial; the emotional inversion (two idiots in a presidential suite crying at an ad) is the gag
jokes.explanation: Good visual irony — the contrast between their luxurious surroundings and their weeping at a low-stakes commercial is funny. The 'Wow! Boy, this is livin', huh?' immediately after implies Lloyd is referring to the presidential suite, the ad, or both — deliberate ambiguity that adds a layer.

jokes.text: Wow! Boy, this is livin', huh? / Yeah. / What's on next? / I don't know. Let me look it up. / Ah!
jokes.setup: They are relaxing in a lavish presidential suite
jokes.punchline: The 'Ah!' implies Lloyd gets a paper cut or stabs himself with the TV guide — slapstick incompetence even in a moment of pure leisure
jokes.explanation: Minor slapstick beat. The TV guide injury implies Lloyd can't even look up TV listings without hurting himself. Functional but lightweight.

jokes.text: Harry, it's Mary! / It's who? / Mary with the briefcase. Mary Swanson. / Swanson!
jokes.setup: Lloyd suddenly sees Mary on TV; he's been to Aspen specifically to find her and didn't know her last name
jokes.punchline: He triumphantly announces 'Swanson!' — the name he could not remember minutes ago, now solved by watching television
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff to the last-name sequence. The accidental TV discovery is both a plot convenience and a character joke — they couldn't find her in a phone book or by thinking, but TV solves it instantly. Lloyd's triumphant 'Swanson!' is a good button.

jokes.text: Lloyd struggles to read 'Host Annual Meeting' aloud, with Harry correcting him letter by letter
jokes.setup: Lloyd needs to read a TV text graphic about Mary's charity event
jokes.punchline: Lloyd cannot parse basic words — 'anool,' 'anewl' — requiring Harry to coach him through each syllable, then needing coaching on 'The' and struggling with 'International'
jokes.explanation: Physical character comedy built on Lloyd's functional illiteracy. Getting stuck on 'The' — a one-syllable word — after struggling with 'annual' is a good escalation. Harry's weary tutorial mode is good straight-man work. Character-specific to Lloyd's profound stupidity.

jokes.text: Well, come on, Cinderella. We've got to get you ready for the ball!
jokes.setup: They've discovered the charity gala where Mary will be; Lloyd announces they'll attend
jokes.punchline: Lloyd calls Harry 'Cinderella' and frames their preparation as fairy-tale glamour — two destitute men with no invitations or appropriate clothes being styled as a storybook transformation
jokes.explanation: The Cinderella framing is a good ironic reference — Lloyd as fairy godmother to Harry's Cinderella, except both are idiots with stolen ransom money. The reference sets up the makeover montage to follow.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd's tuxedo preparation montage — cutting hair badly, shaving, dressing
jokes.setup: 'Pretty Woman' plays as they prepare for the gala — a parody of the classic makeover montage
jokes.punchline: The scissors snipping, loud buzzing, and grinding sounds during the montage imply the results will be disastrous rather than glamorous
jokes.explanation: The 'Pretty Woman' soundtrack is doing ironic parody work — it's the standard montage song for aspirational transformation, applied here to two men who will inevitably look terrible. The grinding and buzzing sounds add audio cues that the transformation is going wrong. Good structural irony that pays off with the reveal at the end of the montage.

jokes.text: During the grooming montage, a loud grinding sound is heard — implying Lloyd is using some catastrophically wrong tool on Harry.
jokes.setup: Lloyd is giving Harry a makeover — haircut, grooming — to prepare for the charity event.
jokes.punchline: An industrial grinding sound accompanies 'Mercy!' from the music — suggesting Lloyd has done something catastrophically wrong to Harry's hair or face.
jokes.explanation: A visual/sound gag that relies heavily on what we see (which the transcript can only suggest). The grinding sound cue and 'Mercy!' lyric timing is a deliberate comedic beat in the montage. The payoff would be visual (Harry's haircut). Moderate.

jokes.text: The reveal of Harry and Lloyd in their tuxedo outfits — presumably garish and mismatched
jokes.setup: The makeover montage has built expectation; 'Pretty Woman' reaches its final note
jokes.punchline: The final visual — their actual outfits (from context, clearly not normal tuxedos) — is the payoff to the entire preparation sequence
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff to the extended 'Pretty Woman' sequence. The film's iconic tuxedo reveal (powder blue and orange) is a pure visual gag that earns its laugh from the extended setup and subverted expectations. Rewatch bonus is high because knowing what's coming makes the anticipation funnier.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd attend a $500-a-plate charity dinner and, when told the price, Lloyd says 'Put us down for four — in case we want seconds.'
jokes.setup: An event coordinator scolds them for crashing a $500-a-plate dinner, expecting them to leave embarrassed.
jokes.punchline: Lloyd misunderstands 'per plate' as a price per course, so he orders four plates 'in case we want seconds' — treating a charity gala like a diner.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character — Lloyd's obliviousness reads extravagance as a menu price. The 'in case we want seconds' kicker elevates it beyond a simple misunderstanding into genuine comedic logic. High character integration because only a Dumb-and-Dumber protagonist thinks this way.

jokes.text: Lloyd's inspirational pep talk about showing 'class and sophistication' is instantly undercut: 'Oh, look at the funbags on that hosehound.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd earnestly lectures Harry about being classy and sophisticated to impress people at the gala.
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence he spots a woman and blurts out a crude objectification, completely demolishing everything he just said.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection with a crisp structure: the longer and more earnest the setup speech, the harder the fall. The specific vulgarity ('funbags on that hosehound') is oddly poetic in its awfulness and is uniquely Lloyd's voice. The juxtaposition is timed to perfection — 'sophistic—oh, look at the funbags' is a near-perfect comedic sentence break.

jokes.text: Lloyd says he'd like to eat a woman's liver with fava beans and a nice bottle of Chianti, then he and Harry both do the Hannibal Lecter hissing sound together.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just objectified a woman at a high-class event; he continues the gag with a Silence of the Lambs reference.
jokes.punchline: Both men do the Lecter hiss in unison, as if it's a perfectly normal shared social skill.
jokes.explanation: The pop-culture reference (Silence of the Lambs, 1991) was extremely fresh at the time and gets a good laugh. The real joke is that both men do it in perfect unison — implying this is a practiced routine between them. Slightly cheap as a reference joke but the synchronised delivery saves it.

jokes.text: Lloyd says 'Come on, let's go get a couple bowls of loudmouth soup' — his term for martinis at a black-tie gala.
jokes.setup: They are at a formal charity gala and Lloyd wants to order drinks.
jokes.punchline: He calls martinis 'loudmouth soup,' a folksy/idiot malapropism that reveals his obliviousness to the setting.
jokes.explanation: A compact, inventive coinage. 'Loudmouth soup' is funny on its own as a phrase, but it also perfectly encapsulates Lloyd's character — he dresses the part but speaks like a redneck at a truck stop. Good economy.

jokes.text: While the ornithologist gives a solemn speech about the endangered Icelandic snow owls, Lloyd calls out to the bartender: 'Can I have some pistachios, please?'
jokes.setup: A serious conservationist is giving an emotional speech about one of the world's rarest birds to a hushed ballroom.
jokes.punchline: Lloyd loudly interrupts to order bar snacks, completely oblivious to the gravity of the moment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words do the entire job. The comic effect is entirely in the juxtaposition of the grave setting against Lloyd's mundane appetite. The specificity of 'pistachios' rather than just 'peanuts' adds a small extra layer of absurdity.

jokes.text: Lloyd declares his old-fashioned romantic feeling — 'where I'd do anything to bone her.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd uses romantic, idealistic language: 'I'm ready for a commitment... that old-fashioned romantic feeling...'
jokes.punchline: The setup promises a sweet, heartfelt declaration; the punchline is a crude sexual admission delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Harry genuinely affirms it — 'That's a special feeling, Lloyd. Yeah.' — which doubles the absurdity. Lloyd's sincerity is the engine of the gag. The structure is a textbook misdirection: the longer the wind-up, the funnier the crude landing.

jokes.text: Lloyd asks Harry to introduce him to Mary and 'build me up so I won't have to brag about myself later. Tell her I'm rich and good-looking and I have a rapist wit.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd wants Harry to do a wingman introduction to impress Mary.
jokes.punchline: He asks Harry to describe him as having 'a rapist wit' — a malapropism for 'rapier wit' — delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. 'Rapist wit' is a perfect malapropism — it's a real word Lloyd almost knows, it's exactly wrong in the most alarming way, and it's delivered with absolute confidence. High quotability; the joke has legs beyond the film. The surrounding list ('rich, good-looking, rapist wit') is well-constructed escalation.

jokes.text: Harry walks up to Mary at the party and opens with: 'Nice set of hooters you got there.'
jokes.setup: The audience expects Harry to deliver Lloyd's smooth introduction, having just received careful coaching.
jokes.punchline: Harry opens with what sounds like a crudely sexual comment — but then clarifies he's referring to the owls on display.
jokes.explanation: Textbook double-meaning joke executed nearly perfectly. The gap between [73:20] and [73:25] — where Mary and the audience sit with the apparent vulgarity — is timed beautifully. 'The owls, they're beautiful' is the ideal rescue line. Highly quotable. Gets maximum value from minimal words. The beat of silence IS the joke.

jokes.text: Harry explains his expertise is 'canines — dogs to the layperson.'
jokes.setup: Harry is trying to seem knowledgeable and sophisticated to Mary and her stepmother.
jokes.punchline: He condescendingly translates 'canines' as 'dogs to the layperson,' as if 'canine' is arcane expert jargon most people wouldn't know.
jokes.explanation: Compact and character-specific. The joke reveals Harry thinks he's demonstrating expertise by explaining the simplest possible word. The deadpan delivery makes it land harder — he's not being ironic, he genuinely thinks this is helpful.

jokes.text: Harry describes his dog-breeding technique: 'Any unusual breeding? No, mostly just doggy-style.'
jokes.setup: Mary asks about Harry's breeding experience; he seems to be giving a straightforward professional answer.
jokes.punchline: 'Mostly just doggy-style' — a double entendre where 'doggy style' is both the literal position dogs use to breed and an obvious sexual reference.
jokes.explanation: A reliable double-entendre that works because the setup genuinely earns both readings. It's not a subtle joke but the construction is tight. Less original than the 'hooters' beat above but functional and well-timed.

jokes.text: Harry explains he crossbred a bulldog with a shih-tzu. 'What did you call it?' — 'A bullshit.'
jokes.setup: Harry mentions an unusual crossbreeding experiment between a bulldog and a shih-tzu.
jokes.punchline: 'We called it a bullshit' — a portmanteau pun that is both the logical compound word and a profanity.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable jokes in this reel. The setup is clever because it baits the audience into thinking about dog breeds, not profanity. The portmanteau is elegant — 'bullshit' is both the only logical name AND a swear word. Mary's hysterical laughing reaction (then Harry's confusion at her laughing) adds a layer. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Harry laughs hysterically at his own bullshit joke alongside Mary, then immediately pivots to try to introduce Lloyd — only for the conversation to have moved on.
jokes.setup: Harry has just made Mary laugh with the 'bullshit' joke and both are sharing the moment.
jokes.punchline: Harry is so caught up in the laughter that he forgets his mission (introducing Lloyd), and the social moment slips away naturally.
jokes.explanation: More of a plot-comedy beat than a pure joke — it's funny that Harry got so wrapped up in the moment that he accidentally became Mary's date, completely undermining Lloyd's plan. Mild laughs, mostly serves the story.

jokes.text: Mary's stepmother Helen immediately invites Harry skiing with Mary after complimenting his tuxedo, steamrolling over Harry's attempts to introduce Lloyd.
jokes.setup: Harry is trying to redirect the conversation to Lloyd, but Helen misreads Harry's good-natured awkwardness as charm and attraction.
jokes.punchline: Helen enthusiastically matchmakes Harry with Mary on the spot — 'Poor thing, she never gets a chance to get out' — completely hijacking Lloyd's plan.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is situational and ironic — Harry is trying NOT to get the date and is succeeding in getting the date. The escalation of Helen's enthusiasm as Harry hedges is well-paced, though not the sharpest moment in the reel.

jokes.text: Harry tells Lloyd he got him a date with Mary. Lloyd's response: a long, dumbfounded pause before 'I love you, man' — followed by literally kissing Harry on the face.
jokes.setup: Lloyd told Harry to introduce him to Mary. Harry actually got Lloyd a date.
jokes.punchline: Lloyd is so overcome he starts kissing Harry on the face. Harry protests — 'You're kissing me. Lloyd!' — but Lloyd keeps going.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that earns its laughs from genuine character — Lloyd's emotions are always excessive and boundary-free. The escalation of Harry's discomfort ('You're kissing me. Lloyd!') works well. Warm and characterful without being mean.

jokes.text: Lloyd declares 'You're going to be my best man, Harry' and 'We already got the tuxes' — planning his entire wedding to a woman he has spoken to for 30 seconds.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just found out he has a first date with Mary.
jokes.punchline: He's already planning the wedding in full detail, noting the economic convenience that they already own tuxedos.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. The 'we already got the tuxes' kicker is the best part — it's the kind of practical detail that only an idiot would see as a sign from the universe. Demonstrates Lloyd's delusional leaps of logic.

jokes.text: In the middle of Lloyd's wedding planning, there is a loud thud and an owl squawk — the champagne cork has killed one of the endangered Icelandic snow owls.
jokes.setup: The gala has been celebrating the rare snow owls; Lloyd called for champagne to celebrate his 'engagement.'
jokes.punchline: The champagne cork kills one of the two (!) remaining owls — an absurdly dark consequence of Lloyd's celebration, treated as pure slapstick.
jokes.explanation: A supremely well-constructed dark callback. The speech about the owls' endangered status at 71:02 is the setup; Lloyd's celebration kills the bird. The payoff is the gangsters' baffled reaction ('How could anybody whack a bird with a cork? These guys aren't just anybody. They're good.') which escalates the joke in an entirely unexpected direction. The juxtaposition of Lloyd's oblivious joy with catastrophic ecological damage is Farrelly-brothers comedy at its best.

jokes.text: Harry looks at the dead owl and deadpans: 'Boy, this party really died.'
jokes.setup: The party has been thrown into chaos by the death of an endangered owl.
jokes.punchline: Harry's response is an awful pun/understatement: 'this party really died' — a double meaning that is both literal (the bird died) and a cliché assessment of a bad party.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. Four words, double meaning, delivered deadpan. The joke rewards Harry's established obliviousness — he doesn't realize his friend just killed an endangered animal, he just notices the vibe has changed. Great timing.

jokes.text: The gangsters interpret the dead owl as a mob message: 'We killed their bird. Now they killed one of ours.' 'How could anybody whack a bird with a cork? These guys aren't just anybody. They're good.'
jokes.setup: The gangsters are watching Lloyd and Harry, convinced they're hired killers who took out their associate 'Mental.'
jokes.punchline: They interpret the accidental champagne-cork owl death as a deliberate, professional mob hit — and are impressed by the precision.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel. It works on multiple levels: (1) the gangsters' paranoid logic is internally consistent, (2) it retroactively re-frames Lloyd and Harry's idiocy as terrifying competence, (3) 'These guys aren't just anybody. They're good.' is an instantly quotable line delivered with complete conviction. The gap between reality (Lloyd accidentally popped a cork) and the gangsters' interpretation (professional assassin takes out bird with champagne) is a genuinely clever comedic inversion. Approaches an 8+ calibration.

jokes.text: Lloyd alone, fantasizing: 'Mary Christmas. Mrs. Mary Christmas. Kinda catchy, huh, Harr?'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has a first date pending and his mind has already leaped to the wedding.
jokes.punchline: He is literally trying out the name 'Mary Christmas' — a pun on 'Merry Christmas' — as his future wife's name, apparently delighted by the coincidence.
jokes.explanation: A cute joke that depends entirely on character — only Lloyd would take genuine delight in his crush's name being a holiday pun. Light but charming.

jokes.text: Harry gently suggests Mary might not be Lloyd's type after getting to know her. Lloyd erupts: 'She is the love of my life! The blood in my veins! We belong together... till the mountains fall into the sea, till the heavens collide! Or until I get sick of her and need to move on.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd delivers a passionate, increasingly purple romantic declaration about his eternal devotion to Mary.
jokes.punchline: He undermines the entire speech with the kicker: '...or until I get sick of her and need to move on.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. The romantic speech escalates genuinely — 'till the mountains fall into the sea, till the heavens collide' is convincingly overwrought — before the kicker destroys it completely. The kicker isn't just a crude reversal; it perfectly captures Lloyd's character: total commitment that can evaporate on a whim. Good earned vs. cheap score because the setup is genuinely long and committed.

jokes.text: Harry clarifies the meet time: 'She'll meet you there at 10:00 sharp.' Lloyd: 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: Harry passes along the meeting time for Lloyd's date — 10:00 sharp.
jokes.punchline: This is a delayed-payoff setup. The joke completes at 87:21 when Lloyd shows up at 10:00 AM instead of 10:00 PM at a bar. Scored at the setup point; the payoff is joke #26.
jokes.explanation: Scored low here because the laugh doesn't come until later. On its own, this is functional plot dialogue. The rewatch bonus is for knowing the AM/PM payoff is coming.

jokes.text: Harry emerges in an outrageous bright ski outfit. Lloyd asks 'Where're you going in that get-up?' Harry explains they are 'fashionable Euro-trash ski trousers' — essentially skin-tight tights.
jokes.setup: Harry appears dressed for skiing while Lloyd prepares for his date.
jokes.punchline: Harry's outfit is obscenely form-fitting tights, which he insists are sophisticated 'Euro-trash ski trousers' — both a visual gag and a character moment revealing Harry's oblivious fashion sense.
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual gag — Jim Carrey in skin-tight tights is inherently funny. 'Euro-trash ski trousers' is a good coinage. The setup/payoff works but is a standard 'idiot thinks he looks great' bit.

jokes.text: Harry insists his tights are fine: 'it's just a tiny lump. No one'll notice.' Lloyd stares. Harry: 'You're right. I can't go out dressed like this.'
jokes.setup: Harry is defending his skin-tight ski tights as presentable.
jokes.punchline: He mentions a 'tiny lump' — presumably his genitalia visible through the tights — and after Lloyd's reaction decides he can't go out after all.
jokes.explanation: The euphemism 'tiny lump' does most of the heavy lifting. The escalation from 'no one'll notice' to immediate capitulation after Lloyd's silent reaction is well-executed. Lloyd's silent stare (inferred) is the actual punchline.

jokes.text: Harry skiing sequence — dressed spectacularly badly, repeatedly crashing into or startling other skiers, with someone yelling 'Nice going, buddy!'
jokes.setup: Harry has changed into a new ski outfit and hits the slopes.
jokes.punchline: His skiing is chaotic and reckless; he provokes 'Nice going, buddy!' from an irritated fellow skier, treated as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: Generic slapstick sequence. The 'Nice going, buddy' is mild. This section is primarily transitional — establishing Harry on the slopes — with modest comedic content. Below the reel's average.

jokes.text: Harry on ski lift: a lift attendant compliments his outfit ('Beautiful outfit, sir') and Harry tips him ('There you go') as if the attendant performed a service.
jokes.setup: The lift attendant says 'Beautiful outfit, sir' — clearly sarcastic or bemused by Harry's ridiculous ski attire.
jokes.punchline: Harry takes it as a sincere compliment and tips the man, completely missing the irony.
jokes.explanation: A compact character beat. Harry tipping the attendant for a sarcastic compliment perfectly embodies his cluelessness. Short and efficient.

jokes.text: Harry crashes face-first into something (inferred) on the ski slope. Mary calls out 'Harry?' and Harry replies from off-screen, voice muffled: 'Oh yeah, I do this all the time.'
jokes.setup: Harry and Mary are skiing together; we hear a crash and grunting.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh yeah, I do this all the time' — delivered muffled (face in snow), presented as reassurance.
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy beat with a good muffled-voice gag. 'I do this all the time' as reassurance that actually makes things worse is a solid comedic instinct. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Lloyd has been waiting at the lobby bar. He asks a passerby if it's 10:00 AM. It's 1:00 PM. Lloyd's response: 'That's what I have too. Thought maybe it was fast.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has been waiting three hours at the bar, clearly concerned he's being stood up.
jokes.punchline: He asks the time, is told it's 1:00 PM, and says 'That's what I have too. Thought maybe it was fast' — implying he's been fully aware it's 1 PM but hoping his watch was running three hours fast.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed. Lloyd's self-delusion is at its most pitiable — he's been sitting there for three hours telling himself his watch might be three hours fast. The logic is internally consistent for an idiot and the delivery would be devastating in its sadness/comedy.

jokes.text: Lloyd rationalizes that Mary is only 'a couple hours' late because 'she's excited about something and everything has to be perfect.'
jokes.setup: Mary is now three hours late for their 10 AM date and Lloyd is rationalizing.
jokes.punchline: His optimistic explanation — she's taking time to look perfect — is heartbreaking and funny because the audience knows she simply forgot/didn't come.
jokes.explanation: More cringe-sad than laugh-out-loud funny. Lloyd's optimism in the face of obvious rejection is a character-comedy beat that lands emotionally but doesn't have a sharp punchline.

jokes.text: Lloyd, still waiting at the bar, says 'This one's on me.' He slides a drink down the bar. The bartender says flatly: 'Yippee.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has been nursing drinks at the bar for three hours waiting for his date.
jokes.punchline: He attempts a big-spender gesture — 'This one's on me' — and the bartender's withering 'Yippee' deflates it completely.
jokes.explanation: The bartender's dry 'Yippee' is the entire joke and it's very well-timed. The pathetic Lloyd trying to be magnanimous while being stood up is a good character beat. Economy is high — one word does all the work.

jokes.text: A woman sits next to Lloyd at the bar and launches into her problems with her ex. Lloyd sits there listening to this stranger monologue about her breakup while he is being stood up.
jokes.setup: Lloyd is at rock-bottom, being stood up at a bar.
jokes.punchline: A total stranger immediately starts unloading her relationship trauma on him — a simultaneous comedy of manners and of situational irony.
jokes.explanation: Transitional cringe-comedy. Lloyd being the accidental therapist for a stranger's heartbreak while nursing his own rejection is mildly funny but not sharply constructed. Functions more as a plot/mood beat.

jokes.text: Harry crashes spectacularly on the ski slope — something involving his face/head — and Mary rushes to him asking 'My God, does it hurt?' Harry, clearly injured and in pain, says: 'I'm fine. I saved a seat for you.' (Pats bench next to him.)
jokes.setup: Harry has had a painful-looking crash; Mary runs to help.
jokes.punchline: Despite obvious injury, Harry's priority is seating arrangements — he pats the spot next to him with 'I saved a seat for you,' treating the crash as a planned social opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy beat. 'I saved a seat for you' is a nicely specific line — not just 'I'm fine' but a redirect to social hospitality mid-injury. The tap of the bench is the visual punctuation.

jokes.text: Mary insists on pulling Harry's dislocated/stuck limb free. She says it'll 'only hurt for a moment, like a Band-Aid.' Despite Harry's protests, she yanks it, producing a horrific crackling sound.
jokes.setup: Harry is injured; Mary cheerfully volunteers to fix it.
jokes.punchline: The 'like a Band-Aid' minimization is immediately destroyed by the prolonged, agonized crackling sound — clearly not like a Band-Aid.
jokes.explanation: Standard cringe-slapstick. The setup is familiar (cheerful helper makes things worse) but the extended crackling sound is a good sound-design gag. Functional but not inventive.

jokes.text: Lloyd asks the bartender if he knows a Mary Swanson. Bartender says she comes in 'all the time.' Lloyd interprets this as an aspersion on her character: 'What's that supposed to mean?' Bartender: 'She has dinner.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd, paranoid and emotionally raw from being stood up, asks about Mary.
jokes.punchline: He interprets the innocent phrase 'comes in all the time' as meaning she's a barfly or a loose woman; the bartender deflates it with 'She has dinner.'
jokes.explanation: Very good character comedy. Lloyd's jealous, paranoid leap — hearing 'comes in all the time' as moral condemnation — is a perfect expression of his insecurity and idiocy. The bartender's flat 'She has dinner' is an ideal corrective. Good economy.

jokes.text: Lloyd learns Mary lives on Alpine Drive. He reacts with incredulous joy: 'No way! That's great! We landed on the moon!'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has been told Mary's address is on Alpine Drive.
jokes.punchline: 'We landed on the moon!' — Lloyd's expression of amazed joy is completely disproportionate and nonsensical, treating learning someone's address as equivalent to a historic scientific achievement.
jokes.explanation: The 'We landed on the moon' non-sequitur is pure Lloyd — he uses cultural touchstones at random to express maximum emotion. Specific enough to be quotable, absurd enough to be funny. The energy of the delivery would sell this in the film.

jokes.text: Harry's speech is comically slurred after a day of drinking on the slopes with Mary: 'Blell, blit blas... it was my pleasure, Mary.'
jokes.setup: Harry is talking to Mary after their ski date.
jokes.punchline: His speech is severely slurred from drinking — 'Blell, blit blas' — but he powers through as if speaking normally.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy through vocal performance. Jim Carrey's slurred nonsense syllables are funny but it's a standard drunk-speech gag without additional invention.

jokes.text: Harry and Mary agree on a dinner pickup time. Mary: '7:45?' Harry: 'Well, I've got a few things to take care of first. Why don't we make it quarter to 8:00?' Mary laughs; Harry is confused.
jokes.setup: Mary suggests Harry pick her up at 7:45 for dinner.
jokes.punchline: Harry 'renegotiates' to 'quarter to 8:00' — which is exactly the same time — apparently unaware they are identical.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the reel. The stupidity is precise and specific — Harry doesn't know that '7:45' and 'quarter to 8:00' are the same thing, but he delivers it with the authority of a busy professional making a concession. Mary's laughter and Harry's confusion at her reaction is the perfect button. This approaches the 8.0 anchor — it's compact, character-specific, structurally elegant, and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd discuss why Mary didn't show up. Lloyd: 'I just figured she was a raging alcoholic.' Both men laugh hysterically, as if this is the funniest possible explanation.
jokes.setup: Harry logically points out that no one would schedule a bar date at 10 AM — it must have meant 10 PM.
jokes.punchline: Lloyd explains he had assumed Mary was a 'raging alcoholic' — and apparently this was an entirely acceptable date scenario in his mind. Both men find this hilarious.
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny. The joke is not just that Lloyd assumed she was alcoholic — it's that this didn't dissuade him from wanting to date her. 'Raging alcoholic' as a neutral dating-profile detail is a good dark-comedy beat. Their shared laughter at it is weirdly endearing.

jokes.text: Harry: 'Oh, God. That's funny. That's good stuff. Oh, boy.' Then immediately: 'Well, looks like you got your night planned, so I'm just going to head out and catch a flick.'
jokes.setup: Harry has just been laughing heartily at Lloyd's raging alcoholic joke and the whole situation.
jokes.punchline: He transitions instantly from genuine laughter to casual departure — 'catch a flick' — as if the whole absurd situation was just mild amusement and now it's movie time. The bathos of the pivot is funny.
jokes.explanation: Minor beat — Harry's casual normalization of the absurd situation is consistent with the film's humor but it's a connective beat, not a standout joke.

jokes.text: Lloyd tells Harry he's always liked him because 'you're a regular guy' — then immediately reveals he's about to dose Harry's drink with laxatives.
jokes.setup: Lloyd gives Harry a warm, genuine-seeming compliment: 'You know why I like you, Harry? Because you're a regular guy.'
jokes.punchline: 'Yep, that's why I want you to stay regular' — immediately followed by showing the laxative box, revealing the entire speech was leading to this sabotage.
jokes.explanation: Structurally the best joke in the reel. The word 'regular' does double-duty as both an affectionate character description and a bowel-movement reference, and the transition between the two meanings is seamless. Lloyd's warm-friend routine as a setup for poisoning Harry is a beautiful piece of dark misdirection. '½ teaspoon for fast, effective relief' as the button is perfect. High marks across all craft dimensions — the pun is earned by the structure, not lazy.

jokes.text: Lloyd toasts: 'To my friend Harry... the matchmaker.' Harry drinks the entire laxative-laced drink cheerfully.
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just dosed Harry's drink with laxatives. He raises a toast to Harry.
jokes.punchline: Harry drinks the entire thing with happy 'Mm-hmm, mm-hmm' sounds — the audience knows what's coming; Harry does not.
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is working hard here — the audience's dread/anticipation of the upcoming consequences is funny. Harry's contented 'Mm-hmm, mm-hmm' is the perfect oblivious-victim sound. The rewatch bonus is high because this sets up obvious physical comedy to come.

jokes.text: Harry's stomach begins violently rumbling — audibly — while he waits alone in Mary's house.
jokes.setup: Harry has just drunk an entire laxative-spiked cocktail and arrived at Mary's house for their date.
jokes.punchline: His stomach rumbles loudly and violently, right on schedule — the laxatives are activating at the worst possible moment.
jokes.explanation: The setup of the reel's final gag. The stomach rumble is a purely physical comedy beat, but it earns its laughs from the anticipation built by the laxative scene. The timing (he's just entered Mary's house) is excellent. Primarily works as a cliffhanger button for the sequence.

jokes.text: Harry is alone in Mary's house. Mary calls down that she's almost ready. Harry's stomach violently gurgles — the reel ends on this sound with the door to Mary's private home still open.
jokes.setup: Harry has drunk the laxative-dosed drink and is now trapped alone in Mary's upscale home with nowhere to go.
jokes.punchline: The scene ends on Harry's stomach gurgling violently with Mary's cheerful 'I'm almost ready!' from upstairs — the looming catastrophe hanging in the air.
jokes.explanation: A strong reel-ending button. The comedy is entirely in anticipation and cringe — the audience knows exactly what's going to happen, and Mary's cheerful obliviousness makes it worse. The scene ends at the peak of dramatic irony, leaving the audience imagining (and dreading) the punchline. Well-structured cliffhanger comedy.

jokes.text: Opening sputtering sounds — the scooter/moped struggling audibly before any dialogue
jokes.setup: Two cross-country travelers arriving in Aspen, presumably in style
jokes.punchline: The pathetic sputtering of their absurd vehicle undercuts any sense of arrival grandeur
jokes.explanation: The running gag of the pathetically underpowered scooter pays off visually on arrival. Functional but not remarkable.

jokes.text: Harry is caught having used Mary's broken toilet, then claims he was 'just shaving' — the visual of shaving on the toilet is implied
jokes.setup: Mary warns Harry the toilet is broken right before he emerges from the bathroom; Harry has clearly just had a catastrophic bathroom incident
jokes.punchline: Harry insists he was 'just shaving' — to save time — implying he shaves on the toilet as a normal routine
jokes.explanation: Classic Farrelly setup: the broken toilet is established mid-crisis. Harry's excuse ('I was shaving — saves time') is a perfect character-specific deflection that reveals his obliviousness. The audience doesn't need the visual because the implication is vivid enough. Strong character integration — only Harry would think this was a plausible cover story.

jokes.text: Harry reacts with horror to the toilet situation after Mary leaves — laughs maniacally at the chaos he's caused
jokes.setup: Harry has just barely covered up his broken-toilet incident with an absurd lie; Mary has left the room
jokes.punchline: Harry bursts into maniacal laughter alone, undercut by whimsical music — a release of pure id-driven relief/chaos
jokes.explanation: The maniacal laugh sells Harry's obliviousness — he's relieved rather than ashamed. It's a good character beat but relies on performance; as written it's functional escalation of the toilet gag.

jokes.text: TV segment: 'the heartbreaking story of the blind Rhode Island boy who was duped into buying a dead parakeet. I just thought he was real quiet.'
jokes.setup: A TV tabloid show teases its next 'heartbreaking' story with mock solemnity
jokes.punchline: The boy's quoted explanation — 'I just thought he was real quiet' — is a perfect deadpan line that makes the gag land doubly: the dark absurdity of a dead parakeet AND the boy's oblivious logic
jokes.explanation: One of the best incidental gags in this reel. 'I just thought he was real quiet' is an exceptional deadpan punchline — economical, dark, and funny on two levels (the boy's sad naivety and the absurdist image of a 'quiet' dead parakeet). It also scores big on originality; it's not a stock dead-pet joke, it has a genuinely surprising pivot. Loses points on character integration since it's a throwaway TV gag with no named characters, but the writing quality is high.

jokes.text: TV anchor: 'the heartbreaking story of the blind Rhode Island boy who was duped into buying a dead parakeet. I just thought he was real quiet.'
jokes.setup: Harry watches TV while panicking; a sensationalist TV news program teases its next segment about a blind child being defrauded
jokes.punchline: 'I just thought he was real quiet' — the child's matter-of-fact explanation for why he didn't notice the parakeet was dead is delivered deadpan, making it unexpectedly hilarious
jokes.explanation: This is a gem buried in a background moment. The setup exploits the absurdity of tabloid TV; the punchline is a perfect deadpan line that works on multiple levels — the blind boy's logic is internally consistent but reveals the whole tragedy is darkly absurd. 'I just thought he was real quiet' is genuinely quotable and highly original. Close to an 8 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Harry reacts to the TV story: 'Who are these sick people?'
jokes.setup: Harry has just caused a bathroom catastrophe in a stranger's home and is watching a tabloid story about a dead parakeet
jokes.punchline: Harry, completely lacking self-awareness, judges the TV subjects as 'sick people' — he is clearly one of these people
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony well-suited to Harry's character. He has zero self-awareness, and his moral indignation directed outward while he sits in the ruins of Mary's bathroom is a crisp character joke. Brief and efficient.

jokes.text: Lloyd shows up at Mary's door to return her briefcase — 'You left it at the airport, you big goof!'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has driven cross-country obsessively following Mary; she is shocked to see him at her door in Aspen
jokes.punchline: Lloyd frames the 2,000-mile trip as simple customer service ('when Lloyd Christmas drives a woman to the airport, he makes sure she gets all her luggage'), calling her a 'big goof' with cheerful obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Lloyd's total lack of self-awareness about how insane his behavior is — dressed up as professional pride — is a solid character-comedy beat. 'You big goof' is an endearingly dumb insult. Works as payoff for the film's core premise.

jokes.text: Harry desperately trying to flush the broken toilet: 'Come on, flush, you bastard!'
jokes.setup: Harry has been hiding his toilet incident; the doorbell has rung and time is running out
jokes.punchline: Harry is still alone in the bathroom begging the broken toilet to cooperate, his panic mounting
jokes.explanation: A good escalation beat — the toilet problem hasn't gone away and Harry is now in a full panic. 'You bastard' aimed at a toilet is funny because of the target, and the callback to the earlier setup earns it. Not exceptional writing but efficiently funny.

jokes.text: Harry's increasingly absurd bathroom cover stories: 'I'm just cleaning my teeth... I'm gargling.'
jokes.setup: Mary knocks and asks what Harry is doing; he has to keep inventing excuses while still dealing with the toilet
jokes.punchline: His excuses escalate from 'cleaning my teeth' to 'gargling' — both technically plausible but escalatingly desperate
jokes.explanation: Solid escalation of Harry's cover-story spiral. The jump from 'cleaning teeth' to 'gargling' — both mundane, neither convincing — is funny in its pathetic incrementalism. Good cringe comedy mechanics.

jokes.text: Lloyd's speech about his philosophy of luggage service: 'When Lloyd Christmas drives a woman to the airport, he makes sure she gets all her luggage. That's my whole philosophy.'
jokes.setup: Mary is astonished Lloyd drove 2,000 miles to return her briefcase; she asks if he drove all that way for her
jokes.punchline: Lloyd deflects the romantic implication by citing a mundane professional code of luggage return — as if this were a normal cabdriver philosophy, not obsession
jokes.explanation: Very strong character joke — Lloyd's self-important proclamation of a 'philosophy' that amounts to basic customer service is a great encapsulation of his character: grandiose self-regard wrapped around profound stupidity. 'That's my whole philosophy' is a quotable closer. High character integration.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'I know how frustrating it can be to lose a bag.' Mary kisses him. His entire motivation reduced to baggage sympathy.
jokes.setup: Mary is touched that Lloyd came 2,000 miles for her
jokes.punchline: Lloyd explains his motivation is luggage empathy — not love, not obsession, just bag-loss sympathy
jokes.explanation: Funny deflation of the romantic moment — Lloyd's sincerity about luggage is both his dumbness and his sweetness simultaneously. Good character work.

jokes.text: Lloyd's romantic speech: 'I feel like a schoolboy again, a schoolboy who desperately wants to make sweet sweet love to you.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd is building to a romantic declaration; he uses the 'schoolboy' simile to convey innocent excitement
jokes.punchline: He finishes the simile with an explicitly sexual punchline — the 'schoolboy' framing makes it jarring and creepy rather than romantic
jokes.explanation: The setup-punchline structure is tight: 'schoolboy' evokes innocence, then immediately pivots to explicit desire. The juxtaposition creates a cringe-funny moment that is very Lloyd — utterly sincere, completely unaware of the dissonance. The 'sweet sweet love' phrasing is also funny in its melodramatic earnestness.

jokes.text: Lloyd, flustered after being interrupted, blurts: 'I desperately want to make love to a schoolboy.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd's romantic 'schoolboy' speech gets interrupted by Mary's husband; Lloyd tries to re-explain his meaning
jokes.punchline: In his fumbling re-explanation, Lloyd accidentally inverts the sentence to say he wants to make love TO a schoolboy — a completely different and deeply inappropriate statement
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the reel. The structure is near-perfect: the original schoolboy line was already funny, the interruption creates tension, and then Lloyd's re-attempt produces a catastrophically wrong inversion that is SO much worse than what he said originally. The joke earns its shock because it's not random — it's a logical consequence of Lloyd's verbal incompetence trying to fix a mess. 'I desperately want to make love to a schoolboy' is devastatingly quotable and the horrified reactions it provokes are entirely earned. Economy is exceptional — six words do all the work.

jokes.text: Mary: 'I'd say more like one out of a million.' / Lloyd: 'So you're telling me there's a chance. Yeah!'
jokes.setup: Lloyd forces Mary to give him an honest assessment of their romantic chances; she diplomatically tries to soften the blow
jokes.punchline: Mary says one in a million; Lloyd interprets this as genuinely hopeful odds and celebrates
jokes.explanation: The most iconic joke of the film and one of the great setup-punchline exchanges in modern comedy. The structure is flawless: the buildup ('hit me with it, just give it to me straight') creates genuine emotional stakes; Mary's 'one out of a million' is meant to be a crushing rejection; Lloyd's interpretation ('So you're telling me there's a chance!') is simultaneously stupid AND internally logical — he is technically correct that one in a million is nonzero. It works because it perfectly distills Lloyd's character: relentlessly, illogically optimistic. The 'Yeah!' follow-up with the pump of the fist is a perfect grace note. This is a cultural touchstone. Comparable in impact to the vasectomy anchor example.

jokes.text: Lloyd answers the door to a gunman and says: 'Hi. We have plenty of towels. Thanks.'
jokes.setup: An ominous knock at the hotel room door; Lloyd answers expecting housekeeping
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's response — offering towels — is completely disconnected from the threatening figure at the door; he has no situational awareness
jokes.explanation: A clean character-comedy beat. Lloyd's hotel-guest autopilot response to what is clearly a dangerous man is a strong manifestation of his obliviousness. The towel line is unexpected and specific enough to be genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Lloyd, upon learning Mary has a husband: 'What was all that one-in-a-million talk?'
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just been told Mary has a husband — the entire premise of his obsessive cross-country trip collapses
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's first response is to invoke his earlier probability discussion, treating it as the relevant grievance — not the kidnapping, not the gun, but the odds she gave him
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback that deepens the original joke. With a gun pointed at him, Lloyd's primary concern is the logical inconsistency of Mary's one-in-a-million odds if she's already married. His priorities are magnificently wrong, and the callback rewards attentive viewers. Tight economy.

jokes.text: Lloyd, confronted by the gunman: 'Excuse me, gunman, who are you?' — polite and formal in a life-threatening situation
jokes.setup: An armed man bursts in demanding the briefcase
jokes.punchline: Lloyd addresses him with a polite formality as 'gunman' — as if that's just a job title, like 'postman'
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. 'Excuse me, gunman' is a perfect Lloyd line — overly polite, completely unafraid because he doesn't process danger normally, and it treats 'gunman' as a neutral descriptor. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Lloyd addressing the gunman: 'Listen, Mr. Samsonite, about the briefcase...'
jokes.setup: An armed criminal is demanding his briefcase back and threatening to kill them all
jokes.punchline: Lloyd calls him 'Mr. Samsonite' — mistaking the man's name for the luggage brand, with complete earnest sincerity
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully specific stupid joke. Lloyd connects 'briefcase' to Samsonite and addresses the gunman by the luggage brand — it's a very Lloyd non-sequitur that also works as a character logic joke. The formal address ('Mr. Samsonite') in a threatening situation adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: The briefcase is opened to reveal Lloyd spent all the ransom money and replaced it with IOUs, including a hand-drawn car worth '$275 thou'
jokes.setup: The criminal demands his briefcase — presumably full of ransom money — be opened; everyone expects to see cash
jokes.punchline: Instead it's full of IOUs written on scraps of paper; Lloyd explains each one, including a hand-drawn car for $275,000
jokes.explanation: The IOU briefcase is a great payoff to the film's central MacGuffin. The visual of a briefcase full of handwritten IOUs — including a crayon car drawing for $275K — is a strong visual gag that escalates absurdly. 'Might want to hang on to that one' as Lloyd's advice about the car IOU is the cherry on top. Good character integration: only Lloyd would do this and find it completely reasonable.

jokes.text: Lloyd's IOU advice: 'That's a car. 275 thou. Might want to hang on to that one.'
jokes.setup: The gunman is raging at the worthless briefcase full of IOUs; Lloyd is showing him the contents
jokes.punchline: Lloyd sincerely advises the furious gunman to 'hang on to' a handwritten IOU for a car as if offering genuine financial advice
jokes.explanation: The best individual line from the IOU sequence. Lloyd dispensing financial investment advice about his own worthless IOU to the man who wants to kill him is perfectly on-brand. The deadpan delivery ('might want to hang on to that one') as genuine counsel is excellent economy. Separated from joke #17 because it's a distinct and independently funny beat.

jokes.text: Harry calling an airline mid-hostage situation: 'Yes, I'd like a one-way ticket to Amsterdam departing as soon as possible, please... Can I have a vegetarian meal?'
jokes.setup: Everyone in the room is in a tense standoff with an armed criminal; Harry quietly makes an escape plan
jokes.punchline: Harry is on the phone booking a flight out — and his primary concerns are departure time AND dietary requirements, while a gun is pointed at him
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of mundane travel planning (including a dietary request) against an active hostage situation is a very good absurdist beat. The vegetarian meal detail is the perfect mundane escalation — his priorities are completely inverted. Good character integration for Harry.

jokes.text: Harry's fight with Lloyd over Fraida Felcher: 'Don't deny it, Lloyd. Fraida told me the whole sleazy story, Mr. French Tickler.'
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are trading grievances about betraying each other over women; Harry accuses Lloyd of sleeping with Fraida Felcher
jokes.punchline: 'Mr. French Tickler' as Harry's accusatory epithet — a comically vulgar and specific insult that implies a whole backstory
jokes.explanation: 'Mr. French Tickler' is an inspired and specific insult — it implies Lloyd used a novelty item with Fraida and is now being held accountable for it in the middle of a hostage crisis. The specificity is what makes it land; a generic insult wouldn't work here.

jokes.text: Lloyd and Harry's fight escalating to: 'Right on my ass after you kiss it! / Kiss it?! You kiss mine! Both cheeks, both lips, right here!'
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd's argument reaches its peak with both threatening to end the friendship
jokes.punchline: Their reconciliation attempt immediately devolves into a 'you kiss my ass / no YOU kiss MY ass' competition — competing ass-kissing demands delivered with furious sincerity
jokes.explanation: The mutual ass-kissing demand is a classic Farrelly escalation — both characters are equally aggrieved and equally childish, and the specificity ('both cheeks, both lips, right here') turns a stock insult into absurdist comedy through sheer over-specificity. Good character integration because their friendship dynamic is perfectly captured.

jokes.text: Gunman to Harry and Lloyd: 'Now, which one of you losers wants to get it first?'
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are still bickering about whose ass gets kissed while a gun is pointed at them
jokes.punchline: The gunman has been standing there listening to this entire petty argument and can only ask who wants to be shot first
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation of the argument scene — the gunman's exasperation mirrors the audience's. 'Losers' is accurate and funny.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd each volunteer to be shot first to protect the other, then immediately start arguing about who deserves it more
jokes.setup: The gunman asks who wants to 'get it first'; Harry and Lloyd have just been furiously fighting
jokes.punchline: Despite their argument, both immediately offer themselves — but their self-sacrifice turns into a competitive argument ('No you deserve it / Yes I do / No you don't')
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sweet and funny character moment — their friendship is restored instantly when one of them might die, but the restoration manifests as a competition over self-sacrifice. The 'Yes I do / No you don't' rhythm becomes a callback to their earlier bickering pattern applied to martyrdom. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Harry's reason for deserving death: 'Yesterday was one of the greatest days of my life. Mary and I went skiing, we made a snowman, she touched my leg.'
jokes.setup: Harry is trying to convince Lloyd he deserves to die first because he 'stole' Mary
jokes.punchline: His list of 'sins' — skiing, making a snowman, a leg touch — is an absurdly innocent day that he describes as worthy of capital punishment
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The escalating list — skiing (normal), snowman (childlike), leg touch (peak intimacy for Harry) — perfectly calibrates Harry's romantic inexperience and innocence. 'She touched my leg' as the climax of a romantic day is devastating and character-perfect. The deadpan delivery of this as a death-worthy offense is what elevates it. Comparable in structure to the 'Snip, snap' anchor — it escalates to a comically anticlimactic peak.

jokes.text: Lloyd's instant response after hearing Harry's 'greatest day': 'Okay, kill him!'
jokes.setup: Harry has just described his 'greatest day' with Mary (skiing, snowman, leg touch) to prove he deserves death
jokes.punchline: Lloyd immediately switches from defending Harry to condemning him — the leg touch is apparently the line
jokes.explanation: Two words that do enormous comedic work. Lloyd's self-sacrifice evaporates instantly the moment he hears 'she touched my leg' — the jealousy is total and instantaneous, and his reversal ('okay, kill him!') is perfectly timed. Economy score is very high because it's among the most efficient jokes in the reel. The beat lands because we know exactly how Lloyd feels about Mary.

jokes.text: Lloyd, believing Harry has been shot, sobs: 'You killed my best friend, you bastard!' — immediately after the shooter supposedly fired
jokes.setup: The gunman appears to have shot Harry
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's immediate switch from 'okay, kill him' to heartbroken grief — 'you killed my BEST FRIEND' — reveals his spite was superficial and his love is genuine
jokes.explanation: The emotional whiplash from 'okay, kill him' to 'you killed my best friend' is well-executed and character-revealing. Good callback that earns a laugh through contrast.

jokes.text: Harry, shot but alive in a bulletproof vest, says: 'And you're a horrible shot. Lucky me.'
jokes.setup: Harry has just been shot; Lloyd is grieving; Harry suddenly sits up alive
jokes.punchline: Harry's first words after being 'killed' are a mild insult about the gunman's marksmanship — delivered with zero dramatic weight
jokes.explanation: A solid dark-comedy one-liner on a fake-death reversal. 'And you're a horrible shot. Lucky me.' is dry and efficient. The setup (fake death) is well-executed, and Harry's immediate critical assessment of the gunman's aim is a good character beat. Not exceptional but well-executed.

jokes.text: 'But what if he shot you in the face?' / 'What if he shot me in the face? That's a risk we were willing to take.'
jokes.setup: The FBI agent explains Harry was wearing a bulletproof vest; Lloyd asks the obvious follow-up question
jokes.punchline: The FBI agent's breezy admission that a face-shot was an acceptable operational risk is delivered with complete bureaucratic detachment
jokes.explanation: The dark bureaucratic logic of 'that's a risk we were willing to take' — applied to shooting Harry in the face — is a great dark-comedy beat. The FBI agent's total indifference to Harry's potential death is funny and slightly sinister. Lloyd's question sets it up perfectly. Economical and quotable.

jokes.text: Lloyd's wounded complaint: 'How come I didn't get a gun?'
jokes.setup: It's revealed Harry was given a bulletproof vest AND a gun by the FBI; Lloyd was not included in the plan
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's only response to the entire kidnapping/FBI reveal is jealousy about not getting a gun
jokes.explanation: A compact character joke. With all the chaos resolved, Lloyd's takeaway is grievance about being left out of gun distribution. It's a perfect distillation of his self-centered obliviousness — not 'I'm glad Harry's alive' but 'why didn't I get a gun.' Very Lloyd.

jokes.text: Lloyd: 'How come I didn't get a gun?' — his only takeaway from the revelation that Harry was an FBI plant
jokes.setup: Harry explains the FBI equipped him with a bulletproof vest and a gun
jokes.punchline: Lloyd's response is not 'I'm glad you're alive' or 'why didn't you tell me' — it's pure jealousy about not receiving a gun
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical character joke. Lloyd's priorities are always slightly, specifically wrong. This is exactly the question he would ask.

jokes.text: Mary's husband is introduced; Lloyd, still confused, says 'He's got a gun!' and panics
jokes.setup: Mary introduces her husband Bobby warmly; Bobby appears and Lloyd registers him as a threat
jokes.punchline: Lloyd shouts 'He's got a gun!' — either paranoid from the previous events or just spotting the security detail
jokes.explanation: A functional but not exceptional reaction beat. Lloyd's gun paranoia in the aftermath is a reasonable character extension, but the joke doesn't have much independent force beyond situational context.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd's lament: 'First Mary dumps us, then the cops take our nest egg, then our hog breaks down.'
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are walking down a desert highway, dejected
jokes.punchline: Their list of misfortunes includes 'our nest egg' (the ransom money they spent on IOUs and fun) and 'our hog' (their absurd scooter from earlier reels) — they have lost everything and don't quite understand why
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat that consolidates the film's comedic losses into one dejected summary. The euphemisms ('nest egg,' 'hog') for things they never actually owned are good character touches. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Two beautiful women on a 'national bikini tour bus' pull up and ask Harry and Lloyd to be their oil boys
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are walking dejectedly down the road; a tour bus stops and gorgeous women lean out
jokes.punchline: The women are looking for two oil boys to 'grease them up before each competition' — the perfect fantasy rescue for two losers
jokes.explanation: The setup is a classic fantasy-rescue scenario and the audience anticipates the punchline. Its value is in what Lloyd does with it (see joke #31). As a standalone setup it's competent but familiar.

jokes.text: Lloyd tells the bikini girls: 'You are in luck! There's a town about three miles that way. I'm sure you'll find a couple guys there.'
jokes.setup: Two women on a bikini tour explicitly ask Lloyd and Harry to be their oil boys — the perfect opportunity for two lonely men who have just lost everything
jokes.punchline: Lloyd redirects them to a nearby town — completely failing to register that he and Harry ARE the guys they're looking for
jokes.explanation: A supremely well-constructed joke that works on multiple levels. The audience has the information Lloyd doesn't, so there's a double-take element. But what makes it exceptional is that Lloyd's response — giving helpful directions — is entirely in character: he's being courteous and helpful, oblivious to the fact that he's directing them away from himself. The structure is tight (setup → apparent resolution → oblivious misdirect → delayed horror), the character integration is as good as it gets for Lloyd, and the economy is excellent. Earns a high score because it's the perfect encapsulation of Lloyd's character in one moment.

jokes.text: Harry's horrified reaction and chase: 'Do you realize what you've done?' as he runs after the bus
jokes.setup: Lloyd has just sent the bikini tour bus away; Harry realizes what has happened
jokes.punchline: Harry's existential horror is massive and immediate — he chases the bus screaming
jokes.explanation: A solid physical escalation of the previous joke — Harry's reaction validates how catastrophic Lloyd's decision was. The physical comedy of him running after the bus is classic. Dependent on the previous joke for its impact.

jokes.text: Lloyd, oblivious to Harry's chase, calls after Harry: 'You'll have to excuse my friend. He's a little slow. The town is back that way.'
jokes.setup: Harry is sprinting after the tour bus in a panic; Lloyd watches him go
jokes.punchline: Lloyd apologizes for Harry's behavior to the departing bus and again gives directions — describing Harry as 'a little slow' (the ultimate pot-calling-the-kettle-black)
jokes.explanation: The perfect coda to the bikini girls sequence. Lloyd calling Harry 'a little slow' while continuing to helpfully give directions to the girls he just dismissed is a stunningly ironic line delivered with total sincerity. The irony is rich because Lloyd is the one who just cost them the dream opportunity. 'The town is back that way' as a repeated grace note is excellent economy. High character integration because only Lloyd would diagnose Harry's panic as a learning disability while giving directions to women he accidentally rejected.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd's consolation: 'Two lucky guys are gonna be driving around with those girls for the next couple of months... We'll catch our break too. Just gotta keep our eyes open.'
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd have just missed the most perfect opportunity imaginable due to Lloyd's obliviousness
jokes.punchline: They resign themselves to waiting for a 'break,' completely unaware they just had one and destroyed it
jokes.explanation: 'Just gotta keep our eyes open' as advice from two men who literally just failed to notice an extraordinary opportunity is rich situational irony. It's a good closing character beat. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Harry and Lloyd playing tag with increasingly elaborate rules: anti-quitsies, double-stamps, triple-stamps, no erasies
jokes.setup: Harry and Lloyd are walking down the road after all their misadventures; they begin playing tag
jokes.punchline: The tag game immediately devolves into an escalating argument over made-up meta-rules (anti-quitsies, triple-stamp, double-stamp) as if these are established laws
jokes.explanation: The perfect film-closing gag. After all the film's events — guns, kidnapping, cross-country obsession, ransom money — Harry and Lloyd end up arguing about tag rules invented on the spot. The escalating rulebook ('anti-quitsies, double-stamp, triple-stamp, no erasies') is funny because they treat these invented rules with absolute seriousness and urgency. It's the ultimate character encapsulation: nothing has changed, nothing has been learned, they are exactly who they were. High character integration, strong originality in the specific made-up vocabulary.
